result.topic: Predictive Test Selection (Facebook, ICSE-SEIP 2019): are the critique's "~10,000 tests, 99.9% passed" figures real, and is a one-hop bound against over-selection discussed in the literature?

claims.claim: Critique number 1: when Facebook selected every test that transitively depended on a change, it picked around 10,000 tests per change.
claims.what_sources_say: Paper Section I says a change to the mobile codebase potentially impacts tests 'of the order of ten thousands', and that build-dependency selection picks a number of tests 'in the order of 10^4' even though most changes touch only a few files. So 10^4 is in the source, but as an order of magnitude and in the introduction only. The only measured average in the body (Section VI-A) is that transitively dependent targets per change are much greater than 1000 (the paper's symbol is a double greater-than), several times its 230-target cap for the learned model. The Facebook Engineering blog (21 Nov 2018) never says 10,000; it says the approach would run as many as a quarter of all available tests per mobile change. Scope: Facebook's mobile monorepo and a build-target graph, not a call graph.

claims.claim: Critique number 2: 99.9% of the tests that transitive-dependency selection picked passed.
claims.what_sources_say: Paper Section III-B (Metrics): 'almost 99.9% of test targets selected by build-dependency-based selection strategy pass'. The critique's figure is right, slightly rounded up, since the paper says 'almost'. It is a bare statement with no table behind it. Do not confuse it with the abstract's 'over 99.9% of faulty changes' caught: that is the learned model's change-level recall, a different quantity. The blog gives no pass share for the baseline; its 99.9 percent figures are the model's regression-catch rate. Section III-B uses this pass rate to argue that skipping tests that would pass saves most of the cost.

claims.claim: Critique framing: the Facebook baseline was 'every test that indirectly depended on a change' (transitive closure), and the fan-out came through shared 'hub' nodes in the dependency graph.
claims.what_sources_say: The baseline description is accurate: Section I says Facebook chose tests that transitively depend on modified code per build metadata, and kept it because build isolation guarantees no impacted test is missed. The hub mechanism is the critique's inference, not the source's. Neither the paper nor the blog uses 'hub', 'fan-out' or 'high-degree node'. Nearest statements: Section II-A says that in a monolith with few interdependency restrictions, even small changes can impact a large number of artifacts. Section IV-A (the 'target cardinality' feature) says that if files are used in many projects, a small change in them may trigger unexpected behaviour. The blog says end products depend on reusable components that share a small set of low-level libraries, so a change to one makes rerunning every dependent project inefficient. The Fig. 2 caption adds that target-level (not file-level) dependencies make the baseline coarser than code-reference analysis. The paper does not measure per-hub effects.

claims.claim: A one-hop (direct dependents only) selection is discussed in the Facebook paper or blog as a bound against over-selection.
claims.what_sources_say: Neither source discusses a one-hop or depth-limited baseline. The paper's only 'directly depends' wording is the Fig. 1 caption defining graph edges. Its related work (Section VII) covers call-graph, class-level and dynamic selection, all transitive. The paper does use the minimal distance between a changed file and the test as a model feature (Section IV-A) and, citing Memon et al., says distance is important but not sufficient by itself for accurate selection. That is a learned feature, not a hard one-hop cutoff. The Musco et al. call-graph impact study (arXiv 1812.06286) was also read: it uses the inverse transitive closure and never varies depth.

claims.claim: Elsewhere in the test-selection / change-impact literature, limiting selection to direct dependents (one hop) or a small depth is a recognised way to bound over-selection.
claims.what_sources_say: Yes, but as a precision-versus-safety trade, not a free bound. (1) Beszedes et al., 'The Dynamic Function Coupling Metric and Its Use in Software Evolution' (Univ. of Szeged; dynamic call traces; the year is not shown in the extracted text): a cut-off depth d gives infinite d as safe but imprecise, and direct coupling only (d=1) as precise and small but unsafe. At d=1 the impact set averages 13-15% of the safe set's size, at d=2 about 25-35%. Recall reaches near 100% only around d=5-15. They note regression 'firewalls' typically involve only the closest dependents, so d=1 can substitute there. (2) Google, Memon et al., 'Taming Google-Scale Continuous Testing' (ICSE-SEIP 2017; build-target graph): a MinDist cutoff of 10 edges. Executing only targets within MinDist 10 or 6 saved about 42% or 55% of resources, and breakages and fixes sat mostly at MinDist 5-10. That is evidence a one-hop cut would miss most real failures at that scale. They also report affected-target sets as large as 1.6 million. (3) The regression-test firewall idea (Leung and White) retests changed modules plus direct callers and callees; I saw it only in search-result summaries, not the original paper. I found no study that measures a one-hop caller bound on recall in a small codebase.

result.notes:
Both critique numbers trace to the paper. 99.9% is a real pass-rate statement (Section III-B, 'almost 99.9%'). '~10,000' is the paper's order-of-magnitude phrasing in Section I (10^4); the body's measured average is only 'much greater than 1000', and the blog says up to a quarter of all tests.

Caveats on use:
- (1) The figures describe a build-target graph in Facebook's mobile monorepo. They are not a call-graph or import-graph measurement, so they do not show what a hub like AppContext.jsx would do in this repo.
- (2) The hub explanation is the critique's inference. The sources only gesture at shared low-level libraries and 'target cardinality'.
- (3) The critique's 'one hop only' bound is not in the Facebook source. Where depth cutoffs exist (Szeged d=1, Google MinDist<=10), they are precision-versus-recall trades. Depth 1 is explicitly flagged as unsafe, and at Google most breakages sat at distances 5-10.

The blog and ar5iv pages were read through WebFetch's summarising model, so their quotes are less reliable than the PDF text. result.topic: Verifying the critique's two literature numbers: '19–23% of duplicate bug reports are worded differently' and 'keyword search finds 10–18 points fewer of them', plus what Zhang et al. (TOSEM 2023) concluded on BM25-style retrieval vs deep learning

claims.claim: '19–23% of duplicate bug reports are worded differently' (the range exists in the literature and measures wording difference)
claims.what_sources_say: Primary source: Jahan and Rahman, 'Towards Understanding the Impacts of Textual Dissimilarity on Duplicate Bug Report Detection' (arXiv 2212.09976, Dec 2022; the arXiv listing says SANER 2023). It appears once, in the Introduction, hedged as 'according to our investigation, 19%-23% of the duplicate bug reports could be textually dissimilar'. There is no method, no citation and no per-dataset breakdown behind it. What the paper operationalises is different: 'textually dissimilar' = a duplicate pair whose n-gram (n=1,2,3) cosine similarity is below the lower quartile (25th percentile) of its own dataset, repeated for uni/bi/trigrams and intersected (Eclipse 662, Firefox 1,455, Mobile 131 pairs). That is a relative cut, 25% by construction, not a measured absolute rate of different wording. Data: 92,854 Bugzilla reports (2017–2022) from Eclipse, Firefox, and a pooled 'Mobile' group. So the range is real and attributable, but it is an unexplained, hedged estimate, and it describes public-tracker duplicates filed by different reporters, not an agent writing its own store entries. Nothing in the paper says the share varies with store size, so the critique's point that wording gaps do not depend on store size is consistent with it.

sources.title: Towards Understanding the Impacts of Textual Dissimilarity on Duplicate Bug Report Detection (Jahan, Rahman)

claims.claim: Related, closest primary measurement of 'duplicates share no words': '19.2% of duplicate bug report pairs share no terms' (Chaparro et al. 2016), which may be the origin of the 19% end of the range
claims.what_sources_say: Chaparro, Florez and Marcus, 'On the Vocabulary Agreement in Software Issue Descriptions' (ICSME 2016, pp. 448–452; PDF read in full). Data: 8,572 duplicate bug-report pairs from 159 Apache Jira projects plus 5,058 duplicate Stack Overflow pairs, with code, stack traces and code references stripped and stopwords removed. Table II, share of duplicate bug-report pairs with zero shared terms: 33.6% using titles only, 19.0% using descriptions only, 5.1% using title+description. The paper's 19.2% is the mean of those three field choices. Mean of the Stack Overflow rows (27.2, 6.6, 2.8) = 12.2%. On the realistic full-text case (title+description) only 5.1% of duplicate bug-report pairs share nothing. Duplicates that do share words share about 31% of their vocabulary on average. A 2025 student review (arXiv 2507.14396, which I read) repeats the 19.2%/12.2%/31% figures second-hand and cites Chaparro with 'Year' left blank. I cannot confirm the 19.2% is Jahan's source; the match is numerical only, since Jahan cites nothing. Companion paper (Chaparro et al., SANER 2019, abstract read): a basic Lucene detector failed to put a duplicate in the top 5–30 for 34–50% of reports across 20 projects. That is a retrieval-failure rate, not a wording rate, and it involves no embedding comparison.

claims.claim: 'Keyword search finds 10–18 points fewer of them' — literal reading: a BM25 retriever recalls 10–18 percentage points fewer of the differently-worded duplicates than of the similarly-worded ones
claims.what_sources_say: The number comes from the same Jahan and Rahman paper, Section III-A / Table IV. It is the BM25 Recall-rate@100 gap between its 'textually similar' and 'textually dissimilar' duplicate subsets: Eclipse 62.78 vs 52.58 (10.20 points), Firefox 57.58 vs 46.72 (10.86), Mobile 78.00 vs 59.55 (18.45). The text says 'ranges from 10.20% to 18.45%'; the Introduction prints '10.02%' (an internal typo). Caveats read from the tables: (1) only k=100. At k=5 Eclipse is 37.63 vs 37.50, at k=10 43.26 vs 41.27, so the gap is near zero at the depths an agent would actually read. (2) Table V: Eclipse BM25 gap is not statistically significant (p=0.2865, medium effect); Firefox and Mobile are. (3) The dissimilar set is defined by a lexical n-gram cosine score, so a lexical retriever scoring lower on it is close to circular. (4) The paper says it contrasts each technique across the two sets and does not rank techniques. The figure is therefore accurate for what it measures, but it is a similar-versus-dissimilar gap for one method, not a keyword-versus-embedding gap.

sources.title: Towards Understanding the Impacts of Textual Dissimilarity on Duplicate Bug Report Detection (Jahan, Rahman)

claims.claim: The same 10–18 points taken as evidence that keyword retrieval is that much worse than embeddings, so embeddings are needed for the wording gap
claims.what_sources_say: No keyword-vs-embedding comparison appears in the paper. The only embedding-based retriever it tests, LDA+GloVe, did far worse than BM25 in absolute terms on the dissimilar subset at k=100: 18.50 / 8.00 / 15.00 against BM25's 52.58 / 46.72 / 59.55 (Eclipse / Firefox / Mobile), so BM25 leads by roughly 34–51 points. (Table III also says LDA+GloVe is about 38% below BM25 on the whole dataset at k=100.) Its smaller similar-vs-dissimilar gaps (2.00 / 6.49 / 5.50 points) come off a much lower base. The deep-learning model (Siamese CNN, trained on pairs, GloVe embeddings) also loses on dissimilar pairs: F1 gap 10.92 / 8.48 / 10.00 and AUC gap 9.57 / 9.38 / 2.97, on a different metric and task, so it cannot be set against recall. Retraining it with domain-specific embeddings gave mixed results: dissimilar-pair F1 rose 1.18 / 6.56 / 3.21 points while similar-pair F1 fell on Eclipse (−7.24) and Mobile (−4.32). The paper evaluates only BM25, LDA+GloVe and Siamese CNN and says so; it does not test REP, BM25F, DC-CNN, SiameseQAT or any pretrained sentence-embedding model. A web-search summary that quoted the figure (10.02%–18.45%) as BM25's weakness reproduces the mix-up.

claims.claim: Zhang et al. (TOSEM 2023, 'Duplicate Bug Report Detection: How Far Are We?') concluded that a traditional IR approach beats recent deep-learning detectors on realistic data
claims.what_sources_say: Authors: Ting Zhang, DongGyun Han, Venkatesh Vinayakarao, Ivana Clairine Irsan, Bowen Xu, Ferdian Thung, David Lo, Lingxiao Jiang (ACM TOSEM vol. 32 no. 4, DOI 10.1145/3576042; I read arXiv v1, Dec 2022, full text). New benchmark: three years of recent reports from six projects across Bugzilla (Eclipse, Mozilla), Jira (Hadoop, Spark) and GitHub (Kibana, VSCode). Findings: (a) data age and tracker choice significantly change measured accuracy (p<0.01, large effect), state bias does not; (b) REP (2011; an extended BM25F over uni/bi-grams plus product, component, type, priority and version features, 19 tuned parameters) is best on 5 of 6 projects, beating the deep-learning SABD by 22.3% on average in RR@10; on Mozilla and VSCode, the two largest projects, SABD is comparable, and on VSCode it is 9% better in RR@10; (c) Siamese Pair, HINDBR and DC-CNN are fluctuating or weaker; (d) Bugzilla's plain full-text search (FTS, exact word matching) beats HINDBR and DC-CNN everywhere and ties SABD on three projects, yet REP beats FTS by 22.1% to 62.7% RR@10; (e) deep learning may only pay off in trackers with tens of thousands of reports, and REP/FTS should be kept as baselines. The paper does not report the share of differently-worded duplicates, and its Implications note says duplicates in VSCode cannot be decided by title words alone (FTS does poorly there). Limits for this design: the deep models are supervised pair classifiers from 2017–2020 using GloVe, word2vec or HIN2Vec, not zero-shot pretrained sentence or LLM embeddings; REP is BM25F plus metadata, not bare keyword search; trackers hold thousands to hundreds of thousands of reports versus the design's 200-entry store. The 22.3% is not labelled relative or absolute in the sentence I read. The published TOSEM version could not be fetched (ACM returned 403), so I did not check it against v1.

claims.claim: 'Keyword search beats embeddings at this scale' is not established; it depends on the kind of query
claims.what_sources_say: The design's own support (design.md §4.4 line 313; E-07 line 163) is general retrieval work (BEIR, Sciavolino, LIMIT), not duplicate-bug-report studies, and the E-07 numeric trigger is labelled inferred (line 163, KS-R10 line 725). The duplicate-report literature I read leans toward lexical at modest scale but does not establish it for a 200-entry agent store. Zhang et al. favour REP/FTS in small and medium trackers, and Jahan's embedding-style method scored far below BM25. But the deep baselines were supervised and older, and Zhang's own FTS note says title words alone fail on VSCode, so the answer varies by data. Chaparro found the title was the best vocabulary source and that retrieval worked even though duplicates shared only about 2 title terms on average. So 'not established for this case' is fair; 'keyword is worse' is not.

result.notes:
Method: WebFetch returned the arXiv and ojcchar.github.io PDFs as binary, so I extracted their text locally with the box's existing pdftotext (read-only, nothing installed, no files in the repo touched) and read the tables directly. That is how I checked the WebFetch summarizer's table values against the source. Table IV's pdftotext layout is scrambled, but its values match the summarizer's reading. All three papers were read as preprints or author copies: Jahan arXiv v1 (20 Dec 2022; SANER 2023 camera-ready not checked), Zhang arXiv v1 (published TOSEM version not fetched, ACM and RHUL returned 403), Chaparro 2016/2019 author-hosted PDFs. Search-summary text should not be trusted for the numbers; one such summary conflated the Jahan gap with a BM25-versus-embedding result.

Findings on the critique's point 3, outside the numeric brief. (1) Both numbers are real, but the critique reads the second as a keyword-vs-embedding gap, which the source does not support. The honest summary is that about a fifth of duplicates may be worded very differently (an unexplained estimate), and a lexical retriever does worse on them, mostly at deep cutoffs. The design already handles this: design.md line 252 has the solving agent write several wordings including silent symptoms (write-time doc2query), and the failure-mode records for ex3 name the 'double charge' vs 'duplicate payment row' mismatch. (2) The critique says the embedding rule 'was wrong' because it was about size, but D16 (line 704) is 'about 5% missed-entry-existed over 50 lookups, OR more than about 1,000 entries', and §4.5 line 317 defines `v_missed_existing`, classified by cause (typo, vocabulary, handle gap). Five percent of 50 lookups is 2.5 misses, so the critique's 'three or more real wording misses' is nearly the same trigger. The design's miss rule is a measured one, not a size rule; the real difference is only whether Opus does a record-time 'should an existing entry have matched?' check, which I did not look for in the design. The wording-gap evidence is a reason to keep that trigger and its measurement (lines 317, 704), not to bring embeddings forward.

result.topic: What the retrieval literature establishes about lexical (BM25) vs dense retrieval at tiny scale: a check of design §4.4 (line 313) against the critique's point 3

claims.claim: BEIR (Thakur et al. 2021) supports 'BM25 is the robust baseline' (design §4.4, line 313).
claims.what_sources_say: Abstract: 18 public datasets, zero-shot; BM25 is 'a robust baseline'; re-ranking and late-interaction models give the best average zero-shot results at high compute cost; dense and sparse retrievers are cheaper but often trail. The fetched Table 2 (averages computed by the fetch summariser, not printed in the paper) puts BM25 at about 0.423 nDCG@10, DPR 0.237, ANCE 0.389, TAS-B 0.415, GenQ 0.410, docT5query 0.434, ColBERT 0.431, BM25+CE 0.476. The dense models are 2020-21 vintage. Dense models beat BM25 on NQ (ANCE 0.446 vs 0.329), DBPedia, ArguAna and Quora (ANCE 0.852 vs 0.789; Quora is duplicate-question retrieval). BM25 trails neural models by roughly 7-18 points in-domain on MS MARCO. The authors attribute BM25's edge largely to out-of-distribution shift and note that many BEIR datasets have a lexical bias in their annotation pools. Adding missing judgments on TREC-COVID raised ANCE from 0.654 to 0.735, above BM25's 0.668. Corpora run from 3,633 to about 15M documents, so BEIR has no tiny-store setting. Newer evidence cuts against the design: the E5 abstract says E5 'is the first model that outperforms the strong BM25 baseline on the BEIR retrieval benchmark' without labelled data. Design E-07 F22 itself lists bge-small-en-v1.5 at MTEB retrieval average 51.68. BEIR supports 'BM25 is a strong zero-shot baseline against 2021 dense models'. It does not support 'at this scale', and it does not cover the modern embedder the design would pin.

claims.claim: Sciavolino et al. 2021 shows dense retrievers fail on the entity-like tokens defect text is made of (design §4.4).
claims.what_sources_say: Finding: on EntityQuestions (24 Wikidata relations, up to 1,000 questions each, e.g. 'Where was [E] born?'), top-20 accuracy macro-averaged is DPR (NQ) 49.7%, DPR (multi-dataset) 56.7% and BM25 72.0%. For place-of-birth it is DPR 25.4% vs BM25 75.3%. DPR is good on common entities and degrades on rare ones; BM25 is less sensitive to entity frequency. Scope limits: (1) The retriever is the 2020 DPR, trained on NQ or four QA sets, plus REALM. No modern embedder was tested. (2) BM25 does not win everywhere: DPR (NQ) beats it on 'famous for', 'author of' and 'country located in'. DPR (multi) also beats it on 'country created in'. (3) Fine-tuning DPR on the question pattern lifts place-of-birth from 25.4% to 73.9%, so the gap is a training-distribution effect rather than something inherent. (4) The popularity analysis covers only three relations. (5) The paper tests Wikipedia entity names in factoid questions. It never tests error codes, file paths, symbols or log lines. The lane evidence marks the mapping to error codes and symbols as the lane author's inference (lane-T-03.md F11 line 78: 'my application, inferred'). Design §4.4 drops that qualifier and states the mapping as fact. The finding is real, but the transfer to defect text is inferred. It also says nothing about silent symptoms, where the query has no rare identifier at all.

claims.claim: LIMIT is evidence that dense retrieval 'fails on exactly the entity-like tokens defect text is made of' (design §4.4 lists it as support for that clause).
claims.what_sources_say: The paper attributes the failure to embedding dimensionality relative to the number of distinct top-k subsets that must be reachable (a sign-rank / combinatorial bound), not to entity or rare-token handling. It also shows the failure is not a domain-shift effect: training on the LIMIT train split barely helps. The task is synthetic, with documents like 'Name likes [a list of attributes]' of about 100 tokens and queries like 'who likes X?'. BM25 is near-perfect, and a token-wise TF-IDF baseline gets 100% by reverse-engineering the construction. The failure needs a qrel matrix in which all pairs of the 46 documents must be retrievable as a top-2 set. A store with one best entry per symptom has no such structure. The theory covers single-vector embeddings only. The free-embedding experiments optimise directly on the test qrels and the authors say they 'will not generalize to a new dataset'. The authors also say lexical models are 'not a panacea'. In their synonym-substituted ablation BM25 dropped by more than 89% and fell below most single-vector models, while Qwen3 Embedding dropped 38.9%. That result favours the critique on vocabulary mismatch. LIMIT supports 'small does not make dense win'. It does not support the entity-token mechanism the sentence attaches it to.

claims.claim: There is 2024-2026 evidence specifically on lexical vs dense retrieval for error messages, stack traces, logs or code identifiers.
claims.what_sources_say: I found no head-to-head benchmark of BM25 vs dense retrieval on error messages or log lines in 2024-2026. The closest are indirect. (1) CoIR (10 retrievers, 10 code datasets): BM25 averages 29.79 NDCG@10, the lowest of the ten. Dense models range from 36.40 (Contriever) to 56.26 (Voyage-Code-002). BM25 is weakest on text-to-code and code-to-text (CodeSearchNet 26.75, APPS 0.95). It is competitive on CodeFeedback-MT (34.73, beating 7 of 9 dense models) and CodeTrans-Contest (50.13, beating 5 of 9). The authors do not analyse BM25 vs dense explicitly. (2) 'Practical Code RAG at Scale' (arXiv 2510.20609): per the abstract, BM25 with word-level splitting is 'the most effective and practical' for code-to-code retrieval. For natural-language-to-code, dense encoders consistently beat sparse, at about 100x the latency. (3) 'Not All RAGs Are Created Equal' (arXiv 2605.14503): the abstract reports BM25 'exceptionally robust performance across diverse tasks' (code generation, summarization, repair), with no head-to-head numbers in the abstract and no stated reason. (4) Long Code Arena bug localization (natural-language issue to repository files; median 331 files): GTE 0.33 MAP and Mistral 0.30, with BM25 and the other retrievers below 0.25 MAP. A search snippet gave different R@1 numbers (0.37/0.35 vs BM25 0.17) that I could not reconcile with the page. (5) dedupT (arXiv 2508.19449, stack-trace crash dedup): a fine-tuned transformer reaches MRR 0.742-0.791 against TF-IDF 0.604-0.693 and TraceSim 0.704-0.752. It has no BM25 arm and no off-the-shelf small embedder. (6) Logs: SecEncoder has no BM25 baseline and LogQA predates the window; both were seen only as search snippets. The only claim that dense fails on error codes and identifiers came from a 2026 practitioner blog (snippet only). Code-retrieval evidence is task-dependent. Dense wins when the query is natural language. BM25 holds up for identifier-heavy and code-to-code queries. None of it tests error strings or tiny stores.

claims.claim: Dense retrieval helps on short natural-language symptom descriptions with a vocabulary mismatch (the premise of critique point 3).
claims.what_sources_say: Supporting: BEIR shows dense models beating BM25 on NQ, DBPedia, ArguAna and Quora (duplicate-question retrieval), all of which are natural-language and paraphrase-heavy. LIMIT's synonym ablation drops BM25 by more than 89% against 38.9% for Qwen3 Embedding. The duplicate-bug-report study shows BM25 loses 10-18 points of recall@100 on textually dissimilar duplicates (BM25 only, no dense arm). In code retrieval, dense encoders win natural-language-to-code (Practical Code RAG; CoIR). Against or unresolved: (a) no source I fetched measures dense vs BM25 on symptom-style queries over a corpus of tens to hundreds of documents. (b) The duplicate-bug paper's domain-embedding result is mixed. (c) Where recall is judged on a short list over a store this small, the shortlist can cover a large share of the corpus, so the recall difference may matter less than ranking and abstention quality (my inference, not from a source). (d) Search-result sources on hybrid search are vendor and practitioner blogs, and they say to measure on your own queries. The premise is directionally right, but its size at about 100 entries is unmeasured by anyone.

claims.claim: Design: 'write-time paraphrase and action handles capture most of the vocabulary-mismatch benefit' (§4.4; E-07 F07).
claims.what_sources_say: The cited evidence, doc2query (Nogueira et al. 2019), shows that appending predicted queries lets lexical retrieval approach much costlier neural re-rankers on MS MARCO-style passage ranking (lane-E-07.md F07, line 70). It does not quantify 'most of the benefit' against dense retrieval, and it is not about human-written paraphrases of defects. In the BEIR data I fetched, docT5query averages 0.434 against BM25's 0.423, about +1.6% (summariser arithmetic). A secondary summary says docT5query beat BM25 on 11 of 18 datasets (snippet only). That is a modest average gain, not 'most' of the dense advantage. The write-time design may still be reasonable. The word 'most' is not established, and the design's own v_missed_existing view (line 317) is the only thing that would measure it.

sources.title: BEIR overview on alphaxiv (docT5query beat BM25 on 11/18 datasets)

claims.claim: Overall verdict on the design sentence (§4.4, line 313): 'BM25 is the robust baseline at this scale and dense retrieval fails on exactly the entity-like tokens defect text is made of.'
claims.what_sources_say: Fair as a conditioned statement, an overclaim as written. Fair reading: for queries that contain exact rare identifiers (error codes, paths, symbols), lexical matching should carry the first stage. BEIR and Sciavolino show BM25 beating 2020-21 dense models out of domain and on rare entities, and the mapping to error tokens is plausible. The lane evidence labels that mapping an inference (lane-T-03.md F11). Overclaims: (1) 'at this scale': no cited paper tests below about 3.6k documents, and LIMIT is a synthetic stress test. (2) LIMIT is cited for a mechanism (entity tokens) it does not test; the paper blames embedding dimension against top-k combinations. (3) 'Fails' overstates relative underperformance by 2020-21 models that are fixable by in-domain fine-tuning. Modern embedders beat BM25 on BEIR average (the E5 abstract; E-07 F22's bge-small figure). (4) The sentence does not cover the silent symptoms the design itself cares about. Design line 252 and the ex3/ex4/ex6 cases have no error text, so there are no entity-like tokens for the cited evidence to apply to. The lane's own recommendation was weaker than the final sentence. Lane-T-03.md (line 40) says 'no evidence dense retrieval beats BM25 at this scale', which is absence of evidence, and ties adding dense to measured zero-vocabulary-overlap misses.

claims.claim: Critique: ''Keyword search beats embeddings at this scale' isn't established either; it depends on the kind of query' is a refutation of the design.
claims.what_sources_say: Mostly a restatement, not a refutation. The design's own wording already conditions its claim on 'entity-like tokens', and its lane evidence says dense should be added when misses come from zero vocabulary overlap. The critique is right that the sentence reads as an unconditional claim about scale, and that nothing cited establishes it at about 100 entries. Both sides lack tiny-scale evidence on defect text. The critique is also right that query type decides the winner: dense wins on paraphrase-heavy natural language (BEIR NQ/Quora/ArguAna, CoIR text-to-code) and BM25 wins on rare identifiers (Sciavolino, code-to-code). But its own numbers (19-23%; 10-18 points) measure how BM25 does on dissimilar vs similar duplicates, not BM25 vs embeddings. So it has not shown that embeddings would do better here either. A related slip: the critique says the rule for adding embeddings is size-based. Design D16 (line 704) is 'about 5% missed, entry existed over 50 lookups, or more than about 1,000 entries'. Five percent of 50 lookups is 2.5 misses, close to the critique's 3. §4.5 (line 317) already defines v_missed_existing, classified by cause (typo, vocabulary, handle gap). The real difference is when the check runs. The critique wants an existing-entry check at record time; the design measures it from later outcomes. The only thing both camps agree resolves the question is measurement on real queries.

result.notes: Method and limits. Nothing was installed or modified. I used WebSearch and WebFetch only, plus read-only greps of the design, critique and sweep-lane files. Every 'fetched' page was an arXiv abstract or HTML page processed by WebFetch's small summariser model, not raw text I read myself. PDF fetches returned undecodable binary, so I used the HTML versions. Where a number is called 'summariser arithmetic' (the BEIR averages and the +1.6% docT5query figure), the paper's own table has per-dataset values, not the average. Lane-T-03 (line 118) made the same caveat for its BEIR and LIMIT numbers. My LIMIT figures agree with its F10, which is a useful cross-check. The BEIR HTML fetch covered only the first 100,000 of 118,446 characters, and the Long Code Arena fetch covered 100,000 of 247,143. Snippet-only sources: SecEncoder, LogQA, the tianpan.co blog, the denser.ai blog and the alphaxiv summary; I would not rest any decision on them. Two items I could not reconcile: Long Code Arena search-snippet numbers (R@1 0.37/0.35 vs BM25 0.17) differ from the page (GTE 0.33 MAP, BM25 below 0.25 MAP), and Sciavolino's REALM number (19.6% in text vs 59.9% in Table 6). I did not verify the corpus size of Sciavolino's retrieval setting. Short answer to the brief: (a) the design sentence is defensible only as 'exact-identifier queries favour lexical first-stage retrieval' and is an overclaim as written, mainly because of 'at this scale' (no cited study is that small), the LIMIT misattribution (dimension vs top-k combinations, not entity tokens), the unmarked inference from Wikipedia entities to error codes, and silent symptoms having no entity tokens. (b) The critique's 'depends on the kind of query' is a restatement of the design's own condition, plus a valid objection to the unconditional-scale framing. It is not a refutation, and its supporting numbers do not measure BM25 against embeddings. No source I found establishes the winner at about 100 defect entries, so the design's miss-measurement route (v_missed_existing, D16) is the right resolution. One thing the critique does expose: LIMIT's own synonym ablation (BM25 down more than 89%) and the BEIR dense wins support the idea that vocabulary-mismatch queries favour dense.

result.point: Point 3: the embedding trigger (D16) is wrong. Wording gaps come from how symptoms are described, not from store size. "Keyword beats embeddings at this scale" is not established. Fix: make misses visible (Opus checks at record time whether an existing entry should have matched), and add a local embedding model only after 3 or more real wording misses.

misstatements.critique_claim: The embedding rule ties wording gaps to how big the store is ("not from how big the store is").
misstatements.what_doc_says: D16 has two triggers joined by OR. One is a miss-rate trigger: about 5 % "missed, entry existed" over 50 lookups, which is about 2.5 misses, close to the critique's own "3 or more". The other is a size trigger: more than about 1,000 entries. The E-07 lane gives the size trigger's reason: the no-model fallback (an agent re-ranking a 10–20 shortlist, or reading the whole one-line index, about 30k tokens) stops being cheap at that size. It never claims that wording gaps grow with the store. So the critique answers a reason the doc does not give. The size trigger is still empty, but for a different reason: KS-R4 and §4.1 steps 3–4 removed the agent re-rank it was protecting.

what_critique_gets_right: "At this scale" is not established, and the design's own lanes say so. E-07 F08 (lane-E-07.md:72) found only one small-corpus test, 154 FastAPI documents, where hybrid Recall@5 equalled dense-only, and states: "No peer-reviewed small-corpus BM25-vs-dense study found". T-03 F10 (lane-T-03.md:76) calls LIMIT "a stress benchmark, not a workload like ours". T-03 line 21: "benefit at our size unproven". LIMIT shows that a small corpus alone does not make dense retrieval win. It says nothing about queries that share no words with the document, which are the case embeddings exist for. The sweep critic flagged the BEIR and LIMIT figures as read through a summariser (sweep/critic.md:103).

Wording gaps are a property of how a query is phrased, not of corpus size. Nothing that drives a vocabulary miss changes between 15 entries and 1,000. The size trigger cannot detect the failure the miss trigger is meant to catch.

In practice the misses are invisible. `v_missed_existing` needs "a lookup.miss whose later outcome names an entry that existed at lookup time" (line 325). But `ks outcome <lookup-id> resolved|not_resolved|abandoned --note` (line 426) takes no entry id. The write gate's near-duplicate check (line 445) extends the existing entry's handles but writes no event on the lookup that missed. Nothing else connects a miss to an entry that already existed: an Opus reviewer's duties (§7.4) do not include it, and reusing a `root_cause_id` requires already knowing the row exists. So the miss trigger can never fire. The size trigger will not fire at the store's real size (about 15 seeded entries, then lazy seeding, §8). D16 is therefore "never" in effect, and §9's admitted limit goes unmonitored.

Record time is the right place for the check. An Opus author is already present (§7.3, §7.4). §7.7 line 467 costs a record at 5–10k Opus tokens, and records are rare: only escalated cases, cases with two or more failed approaches, or burned builds. The check runs inside a pull verb, so it needs no hook and no install, and it breaks none of the owner's standing constraints.

Counting about 3 real wording misses gives the same number as the doc's miss trigger (5 % of 50 ≈ 2.5). An absolute count is easier to read at this store's lookup volume: KS-9 opens at 20 encounters or 8 weeks (line 659), so a 50-lookup sliding window may take months to fill.

Silent-symptom queries do exist in this repo. For ex3 the only text on screen is the generic toast "Couldn't record payment — please retry" (src/app/providers/AppContext.jsx:324). The defect itself, a second payment row, produces no error text. Any lookup for it is a prose description, which is the kind of query where vocabulary mismatch is real.
result.reasoning:
(a) Is D16 wrong? Its miss-rate trigger is numerically the same as the critique's rule: 5 % of 50 lookups ≈ 2.5, against "3 or more". So the critique does not change the number. It changes what is counted and whether it can be counted. The size trigger (> ~1,000 entries) came from E-07's reasoning about cost. A lexical shortlist re-ranked by the calling agent, or the whole one-line index read by the agent (~8k tokens at 200 entries), stops being cheap past ~1,000 entries or ~30k tokens (lane-E-07.md:43, F29). That is not a claim that wording gaps grow with size, so the critique's line ("not from how big the store is") misses the size trigger's real reason. But the reason is gone anyway. KS-R4 (line 719) and §4.1 (lines 294–295) show at most two cards and do no LLM re-ranking, and §7.1 has no verb that lists the index. Nothing the size trigger protected is left in the design. FTS5 BM25 at 1,000 rows costs nothing more, so the size trigger is dead weight and should go. The real defect in D16 is the miss trigger, and it is worse than the critique says. Two reasons:
(1) It cannot be measured. See (b).
(2) It is mismatched with its own remedy. §4.4 (line 313) adds vectors "fused by RRF for ranking only, never for abstention". §4.1 step 4 (line 295) only admits a candidate on lexical coverage ≥ θ_cand or an exact handle. A query that shares no words with the entry therefore stays a miss even after embeddings are installed. The trigger counts vocabulary misses, and the specified remedy cannot recover a single one.
Also, §4.5 counts typo and handle-gap misses under the same view. Typos belong to trigram matching (already present, and it fails on prose: architect C's "easbuild faild gradel" returned nothing). Handle gaps belong to `proposed_handle` (§4.3). Neither is evidence for embeddings.

(b) Can `v_missed_existing` ever fill? Not as written. The paths, one by one:
- The miss → `ks claim --lookup` → escalation → `ks record` chain does link the miss to the new record, through claim_seq (§7.5).
- The write gate's exact-Jaccard near-duplicate check (line 445) is the only detector. Its Jaccard runs on token shingles, and the doc does not say over which fields. If that means prose, it has the same blind spot as the BM25 that missed. Its output is "extend the existing entry's handles", not an outcome on the miss.
- Reusing `root_cause_id` requires knowing the row exists, and no root-cause search exists.
- The Opus reviewer is not asked to look (§7.4).
- Misses that are never recorded (recording is "never part of a phase's Done-when", line 443) are never examined at all.
So the critique's Opus record-time check is a real improvement to measurability. The detection primitive (Jaccard) is partly there; the link and the classification are missing. It can be made cheaper and more reliable than a bare Opus judgement. The lookup row already stores the internal top-20 with their features (§3.6 line 282). So whether the existing entry was ranked but abstained (a threshold problem, to fix by recalibration) or was not retrieved at all (a vocabulary or handle problem) can be decided mechanically from stored data. Detection should also use a check that does not depend on wording: the §3.7 join from the new fix diff's changed files to existing footprints, plus the draft's own handles run against the store at the miss's index watermark. Opus then only rules on a short list. The cost is about 1–3k extra Opus tokens on a rare event, or about 8k if Opus scans the whole one-line index while the store is small. That fits the Opus budget, needs no install, and keeps the store pull-only. One risk to note: LLM judges are poor at relevance (M-02 30). It is small here, because the ruling is measurement only and the PR's Opus reviewer can re-check it.

(c) Is the doc's claim conditional? §4.4 ties it to entity-like tokens and §9 admits the gap for prose, so "it depends on the kind of query" mostly restates the doc. The overreach is "at this scale" (lines 163, 313), backed by large-corpus BEIR and the LIMIT stress test. The query kinds in this store:
- Error-log lookups (`--log`, the step-zero default, §7.2), `ident`, `tmpl`, `ctx` and `doc_ref`: entity-heavy, where lexical and exact matching are right and dense retrieval adds little or hurts.
- Prose: `--text` symptom descriptions, `--action "<phase Goal>"` against action handles, and the prose behind `--prescription`. Here vocabulary mismatch is real. Examples: ex3's double charge with only a generic toast; architect C's "android build broke" sharing only "build" with ex7 and ex8.
The doc handles prose with write-time paraphrases and action handles (doc2query, E-07 F07). It also gets indirect cover: `--files` footprint joins and the exact `doc_ref` match carry the silent defects (ex3, ex4, ex6) without wording. Note that the repo's own prose is written in one consistent vocabulary ("double-charge" in CLAUDE.md:153, HANDOFF-2026-07-28-open-work.md:257, CODE-MAP.md:110/363/566/673/770). That lowers the mismatch rate compared with multi-reporter bug trackers, but does not remove it for a fresh agent describing a symptom it is seeing.

(d) The figures. I expect them to come from the duplicate-bug-report literature on "textually dissimilar" duplicates: Jahan & Rahman, SANER 2023, reported roughly 22–23 % of duplicates as textually dissimilar across several trackers, with detection degrading on them. The "10–18 points" is probably a recall drop on those dissimilar duplicates. The Research lane must check whether that drop compares keyword methods against embedding methods, or similar against dissimilar duplicates for the same method. My recollection is that deep-learning and embedding detectors also degrade on dissimilar duplicates; if so, the figures prove the gap exists without proving embeddings close it. Those corpora are tens of thousands of reports written by many end users; here the queries are mostly canonicalised tool output and the entries are paraphrased by an Opus author. Even taken at face value, the figures do not overturn "embeddings later, behind a measured trigger". They argue that the trigger must actually be measurable, count only vocabulary misses, and be paired with a remedy that can recover those misses.

(e) Net verdict: partly. The direction is right: the rule is wrong and the misses are invisible. The critique misreads the size trigger's reason and slightly overstates the doc's claim, which was conditional apart from "at this scale". Its fix is sound but incomplete: it needs a write path for the outcome, a mechanical classification of each miss, a detector that does not depend on wording, and a dense channel that is allowed to produce a candidate.
result.recommended_change:
1. Give `v_missed_existing` a write path.
   - `ks record` runs a mechanical reverse check before it creates a new entry, using three detectors:
     - the draft's own handles (prose, action, ident, files) run as a lookup against the store at the index watermark of the miss lookup linked through claim_seq;
     - the §3.7 join from the new fix diff's changed files to existing footprint items;
     - the existing exact-Jaccard check.
   - It prints at most three cards inside the 2,000-character cap.
   - The Opus author rules each one same, related or unrelated:
     - "same" extends the existing entry's handles, as §7.3 already does, and writes a `missed_existing` outcome on the miss lookup;
     - "related" reuses its `root_cause_id`.
   - Add `--entry <id> --cause <class>` to `ks outcome` (§7.1 line 426) so a session that finds the entry later can link it too.
2. Classify each miss mechanically before Opus labels it.
   - If the entry was in the miss lookup's stored internal top-20 (§3.6), the class is `abstained`. That is a threshold matter, reported at KS-9, and does not count toward embeddings.
   - Otherwise Opus labels it `vocabulary`, `typo` or `handle_gap`.
3. Add one line to `ks close`: the count of miss lookups with a claim but no record and no linked outcome, labelled "unexamined", so unknown is never read as zero (RT-06).
4. Restate D16 and §4.5:
   - Only `vocabulary` misses count toward embeddings: the entry existed, it was outside the internal top-20, and the miss was not a typo or handle gap.
   - Report the count as k of n lookups at the KS-9 checkpoint.
   - k ≥ 3 opens an owner install decision on a local embedding channel; nothing is installed automatically.
   - Drop the > ~1,000-entry trigger. Its reason, the agent re-rank of a 10–20 shortlist or the whole index, left the design with KS-R4.
   - Keep the numbers as owner parameters (KS-R10).
5. Amend §4.4 so the remedy can recover what the trigger counts. If vectors are added, a dense-only hit may produce a candidate, never a lead. The rule is rank-based (dense top-1 with a rank margin over dense top-2), not a cosine threshold, matching T-03's no-absolute-score rule. Everything still goes through the gate. Otherwise, under §4.1 step 4, a query sharing no words with the entry stays a miss even with embeddings.
6. Reword §4.4 and §2.2 E-07 to: "no evidence that dense retrieval beats BM25 on identifier-heavy queries; for prose symptom queries (`--text`, `--action`) the benefit at this scale is unmeasured (E-07 F08, T-03 F10)." Name `--text` and `--action` as the query kinds the trigger watches.

open_questions_for_research: Source of the 19–23 % and 10–18-point figures (expected: Jahan & Rahman, SANER 2023, on textually dissimilar duplicate bug reports, or a follow-up). Is the 10–18 points keyword against embedding methods on dissimilar duplicates, or similar against dissimilar duplicates for the same technique? Do embedding and deep-learning detectors degrade equally on them? Only the first reading supports embeddings as the remedy.

Which fields does the §7.3 exact-Jaccard near-duplicate check shingle: prose only, or idents, files and templates too? The doc does not say. Prose-only Jaccard shares the vocabulary blind spot that caused the miss.
Does `node:sqlite` load the sqlite-vec extension? §6.4 leaves this open, and it decides whether the remedy is one install or two.

What share of real lookups in the ship program will be prose (`--text`, `--action`) rather than `--log` error text? Only the prospective log (KS-7 to KS-9) can say, and it sets how often a vocabulary miss can occur at all.

what_critique_gets_right: The design does admit the gap. §5.5 line 349 lists among the things it cannot detect: 'Semantic changes outside the footprint (a new caller passing different input to an unchanged function)'. §9 line 508 says 'an unchanged footprint is necessary, never sufficient'. The winning proposal (architect-A.md:214) and the KS-C8 repo refuter name the same hole.

A new call site in a new file changes no footprint item, so none of the eleven §5.1 triggers (line 331) fires. The conditional first-commit lookup (§7.2 line 438) runs only when the phase's Scope paths intersect an entry footprint, and a new file may not.

A one-hop search for a symbol name is cheap here and needs no install. git grep -w over backend, src and technician-app/src took 80-100 ms per call on this box, and a batched multi-symbol search at origin/main took the same. Distinctive guarded primitives have tiny caller sets: verify_pin has one non-test caller (service.py:97), create_access_token one (service.py:110), compare_secret three (ops/deps.py:44, customer_messaging/router.py:157, service.py:158), app.logPayment one (JobDetail.jsx:680) and run_dispatch_once one (main.py:128).

The hub argument holds for module-level or transitive closure: AppContext is referenced by about 20 src files and useApp by 20. If callers are computed at all, one hop on a function symbol is the right bound.

HR §5 skipped graphify (a whole-repo graph with an LLM pass and a PreToolUse hook, an unpinned package released that day, staleness on cherry-pick branches), not grep-level searches. HR Q3 (line 48) says 'the hot-path call sets are small enough for grep', and HR §5 (line 300) uses grep/ast-grep as ground truth. A one-hop symbol search computed per target inside the CLI is therefore not the 'call-graph tooling' that §1.4 line 109 cites as skipped.

The idea fits the design's existing grain. §3.4 line 269 already records a named caller as a hand-captured precondition (ex3: 'the caller span in JobDetail.jsx unchanged'). What is missing is detection of new callers.
result.reasoning:
(a) The doc admits the gap in §5.5 (line 349), quoted above, and in §9 (line 508). The gap was documented and was raised by the KS-C8 refuter, so this is not a slip of the design.

(b) Walking the critique's ex6 example against the code shows three problems.

- The PIN check is verify_pin (security.py:33). Its only non-test caller is IdentityService.login (service.py:97). The lockout check is is_locked (throttle.py:50), called at service.py:94 'deliberately BEFORE verify_pin'. The lock is cleared at service.py:107-108.
- ex6 is a do_not_apply entry whose check is the protective pytest pair. A 'remember this device' endpoint in a new file that calls verify_pin and resets locked_until without is_locked adds no caller of any symbol in ex6's captured footprint: the login span, the throttle functions, get_for_update. verify_pin is in the fix diff only as a comment. So the blanket mechanism does not fire on its own example.
- If an author had named verify_pin by hand, the entry would go suspect. §5.2 then re-runs the protective tests, which never exercise the new endpoint and still pass. The inject-control mutant on login still flips, so the entry is `reaffirmed` and the trace is re-stamped with the new caller set. The alarm clears itself.
- The phase-close scan runs at origin/main, after the merge, so the most it yields is one 'newly suspect' count in a closing message, with the bug already on main.
- 'Suspect' is the wrong state. ex6's claim is still true: login refuses a correct PIN while locked. The new code violates the rule on a path the protective test does not cover. That is a rule-coverage alert for a reviewer, not staleness.
- If the callers list were made a precondition so that reaffirm is blocked (§3.4 line 269), it would cap ex6 at candidate (§4.1 line 293) until an Opus revision. That weakens the entry's main job, stopping HANDOFF A2's wrong prescription (§7.2 line 437). Clearing it needs a Docker plus Postgres re-verify, which §9 line 511 says is usually inconclusive on this box.
- A realistic device flow verifies a device token and mints a JWT through create_access_token, never touching verify_pin. The guarded set is therefore an Opus judgement per entry, not something capture can derive.

(c) Cost of computing the list:
- git grep -w is built in, takes about 80-100 ms per call (process spawn dominates) and batches many symbols into one call. That adds about 0.1 s per lookup on top of the 23-35 ms freshness check and one call at close. Filtering hits to code tokens can reuse the planned lexer.
- Searching at file granularity catches aliases, because an aliased import line still names the symbol. Test paths must be excluded: test_security.py and test_service.py call verify_pin.
- Common method names (login, get) collide, so this works only for distinctive free-function names.
- Python ast needs an interpreter that is not on PATH (§1.5 line 121), so it would run only in CI or Docker. The TypeScript compiler API couples the CLI to the app's node_modules. ast-grep is the D5 install decision (§11 line 693).
- None of these is the graphify-class tool HR §5 skipped.

(d) The hub argument is right for import closure and mostly beside the point for function symbols, whose one-hop sets here are 1-3. The real over-flag risk is hub primitives at one hop: sendOrQueue is referenced in 13 mobile files and flushOutbox in 8. Every legitimate new screen adds a caller, and that is the correct pattern, so a blanket callers list on every footprint would churn every phase.

(e) As proposed (blanket, every footprint symbol, mapped to suspect) I would reject it: it misses its own example, clears itself when it does fire, fires after the merge, over-flags hub primitives and degrades do_not_apply entries. A modified, opt-in form is worth having at low cost.

- The catch that actually prevents this bug belongs in the repository's CI, through the design's own D17 seam (§11 line 705). That is a backend pytest which walks the code with stdlib ast and pins the closed caller set of verify_pin and create_access_token to IdentityService.login. It fails before the merge, with no install and no store involvement.
- The defences this example already faces are stronger than a store flag: the CLAUDE.md lock invariant, which is always loaded (§1.4 keeps rules as rules); Opus-only routing for auth and PIN (§7.2 line 435); and the PR's Opus reviewer.
- Net: a nice-to-have for after KS-6b, since ex6 is unverified_seed until then. It does not belong on the path to the pilot.
result.recommended_change:
1. Do not add a blanket callers list to every entry's footprint, and never map a caller change to `suspect`.
2. Add an optional footprint item kind, `guarded_primitive`. The recording Opus author names it per entry, only for a distinctive symbol with an expected closed caller set. For ex6 that set is verify_pin and create_access_token, both expected to be called only from IdentityService.login. The CLI computes it at the target with one batched `git grep -w`, filtered to code tokens by the existing lexer, with test paths excluded, at file granularity so aliased imports are caught. No install is needed.
3. A change in that set yields a separate warning, 'new path to guarded primitive X at file:line; entry <id>'s rule applies; its protective check does not cover this path'. It is not a status change. It does not cap the entry, `reaffirmed` cannot clear it, and only an Opus `ks revise` that adds the caller to the expected set clears it.
4. Surface the warning before the merge, inside the pull-only rule. Either the PR's Opus reviewer runs `ks lookup --diff origin/main...HEAD`, which matches the symbols the diff newly references against guarded primitives and `ident` handles (one hop computed from the diff, so no stored list is needed), or this rides the §7.2 first-commit lookup. Either way it is a §7.6/D10 wording change, not a hook. Keep the post-merge `ks close` count as a backstop.
5. Prefer, and do first, the D17 route: when ex6 is verified, promote its rule into a backend pytest that uses stdlib ast to assert the closed caller set of verify_pin and create_access_token. That catches the critique's example in CI before the merge, whether or not the store exists.
6. Amend §5.5 line 349 and §1.4 line 109 to say that one-hop name search for owner-named guarded primitives is in scope and graph tooling is not, and cite HR Q3 line 48.
7. Schedule items 2-4 as optional work in KS-3, or after KS-6b, since ex6 is unverified_seed until then. Measure the false-alarm rate (legitimate new callers per guarded primitive per phase) from git history before turning it on.

result.point: Point 3: the embedding trigger (D16) is wrong because wording gaps come from how symptoms are described, not from store size; "keyword beats embeddings at this scale" is not established and depends on query kind; fix = make misses visible (Opus checks at record time whether an existing entry should have matched) and add a local embedding model only after 3+ real wording misses.

misstatements.critique_claim: "The rule for when to add embeddings was wrong", meaning a rule driven by how big the store is.
misstatements.what_doc_says: D16 has two triggers joined by OR, and it is marked inferred, an owner parameter. Trigger 1 is a miss rate: "about 5 % 'missed, entry existed' over 50 lookups". That is about 2.5, so in practice 3 misses in a window of 50, which is close to the critique's own '3 or more'. Trigger 2 is size: 'more than about 1,000 entries'. KS-R10 lists the embedding trigger as an owner parameter, not a design fact. The rule is therefore not mainly size-driven. Its miss trigger is roughly the critique's rule, minus the 'wording' restriction and minus any defined way to fill the count.

misstatements.critique_claim: "Wording gaps come from how people describe symptoms, not from how big the store is". This presents the size trigger as a claim that wording gaps grow with the store.
misstatements.what_doc_says: Nowhere does the doc tie wording gaps to store size. §9 says any symptom with no word in common with a handle is a miss, at any size. The size trigger comes from lane E-07, and its reason is cost and fit, not wording. The cheap-agent fallbacks are the whole one-line index in the prompt (about 8k tokens at 200 entries; degrades past a few hundred) and the agent re-ranking a 10-20 entry shortlist. The size trigger fires when those stop fitting (about 1,000 entries or about 30k tokens of index). The critique attacks a reason the size trigger never had. The real flaw is different: the final design dropped the mechanism the size trigger protected. KS-R4 shows at most one lead and one candidate, §4.1 says no LLM re-ranking inside the store, and output is capped at 2,000 characters. So the size trigger now has no stated reason at all.
misstatements.doc_ref: §9 line 513; §2.2 E-07 line 163; evidence/sweep/lane-E-07.md lines 11 and 43; §12.1 KS-R4 line 719; §4.1 steps 3-4 lines 294-295

misstatements.critique_claim: The doc asserts "Keyword search beats embeddings at this scale".
misstatements.what_doc_says: Not verbatim. The doc says 'evidence that dense retrieval does not beat BM25 at this scale (BEIR, Sciavolino entity queries, LIMIT)' (line 163). §4.4 says 'BM25 is the robust baseline at this scale and dense retrieval fails on exactly the entity-like tokens defect text is made of'. §6.1 says 'dense retrieval unproven at this scale'. So the doc's claim is 'does not beat' or 'unproven', and §4.4 limits it to entity-like tokens. Line 163 still overstates: the lanes say none of the evidence is at this scale. BEIR corpora run from thousands to millions of documents, LIMIT is a stress benchmark, and lane E-07 found 'no peer-reviewed small-corpus BM25-vs-dense study'. The critique's 'not established' is right against line 163, but its paraphrase is stronger than anything the doc says.

misstatements.critique_claim: "It depends on the kind of query", offered as a correction.
misstatements.what_doc_says: The doc already makes the query-kind split. Dense retrieval is said to fail on entity-like tokens (error codes, identifiers). Prose symptoms are handled by writing paraphrases at record time, a doc2query technique ('several wordings, including silent symptoms with no error text'). Silent defects are handled by `action` verb-object handles ('the only handle for silent defects ... ex3, ex4, ex6'; fails when 'the agent phrases its plan differently'). The doc also admits 'Lexical retrieval only' as a limit. This is mostly a restatement. What the doc lacks is an explicit statement that prose and `--action` queries are exactly where dense retrieval could help.
misstatements.doc_ref: §4.4 line 313; §3.3 prose row line 252, action row line 255; §9 line 513

misstatements.critique_claim: "Make misses visible" implies the design has no miss measurement.
misstatements.what_doc_says: The intent is in the doc. §4.5 defines `v_missed_existing` ('a miss later resolved to an existing entry: the embedding trigger, classified by cause: typo, vocabulary, handle gap'). §4.6 makes it one of the owner's three measurements. KS-9 reads it. KS-A3 says the design adopted C's rule that 'triggers [are] counted only on cause-classified misses'. What the doc never says is how the count gets filled. `ks outcome` takes no entry argument and only resolved, not_resolved or abandoned. The outcome kinds (resolved, not_resolved, referenced, abandoned, gate_absent) have no missed_existing. Nobody is assigned to classify the cause. D16 does not carry the class restriction KS-A3 claims. So the claim is wrong as a description of the design's intent, but right in effect.

what_critique_gets_right: Nothing in the design ever fills `v_missed_existing`. §4.6 needs 'a lookup.miss whose later outcome names an entry that existed at lookup time'. But `ks outcome <lookup-id> resolved|not_resolved|abandoned` (line 426) cannot name an entry, and the outcome kinds (line 280) do not include missed_existing. Proposals B and C both defined how it gets filled. B: the near-duplicate check in `ks record` 'records outcome missed_existing and a proposed handle from the missed query'. C: 'missed_existing is set when a newly recorded entry's exact handles, or a handle-token Jaccard of at least 0.6, match an earlier MISS'. That was lost when the proposals were merged (architect-B.md lines 188/339, architect-C.md line 207). If the view stays empty, the miss trigger can never fire and the owner reads that as 'no misses'.

The part that exists today does not close the gap. The write gate's exact pairwise Jaccard check (§7.3 line 445; KS-2 tests that it refuses a near-duplicate sibling, line 574) does catch that an entry already existed. It extends that entry's handles. But it does not tie the record back to the lookup that missed, even though the escalation path already carries the lookup id (line 435) and `claim_seq` (line 453). And it compares words, so it shares the blind spot of a wording miss, though overlap in cause, fix and identifiers softens that. An Opus author ruling at record time is a real gain in measurability. It costs little inside the 5-10k-token record step (§7.7 line 467), and it is not the 'LLM judge as retain gate' the doc rejects (T-05 line 145): it classifies a duplicate, it does not gate retention.

Only wording (vocabulary) misses should count toward the trigger. This is C's graft, which judge 3 endorsed (judge-3.md line 240) and KS-A3 says was adopted (line 742). D16 (line 704) does not carry it. A typo miss or a handle-gap miss is not fixed by embeddings.

A fixed count of 3 is better than '5 % over 50 lookups'. The KS-9 checkpoint comes at 20 encounters or 8 weeks (line 659), so the 50-lookup window may never fill. Conditional first-commit lookups also pad the denominator. Three also fits the doc's own rule-of-three framing (§4.5 `v_rule_of_three`).

'At this scale' is not established. Line 163 says 'evidence that dense retrieval does not beat BM25 at this scale', but the lanes' own facts say no small-corpus study exists (lane-E-07 F08; lane-T-03 F09: BEIR corpora are 'thousands to millions of documents, none as small as this store'; F10: LIMIT is 'a stress benchmark, not a workload like ours'). §6.1's 'unproven at this scale' (line 381) is the honest wording.

The size trigger is not a sound reason to install embeddings in the final design. Its real reason, the agent re-ranking a shortlist or reading the whole index, is absent from the final design (KS-R4 line 719; §4.1 line 294 'no LLM re-ranking inside the store'). Yet line 163 still cites 'the calling agent's own LLM as re-ranker' as a reason no embeddings are needed.

Seeing a miss has a second, cheaper payoff. A detected wording miss can become a new prose handle through the design's own Rocchio-style document feedback. Today §4.3 (lines 304-305) makes handles only from confirmed hits and refuted ones, never from misses. So without miss detection, the same wording misses again.
result.reasoning:
(a) D16 is not 'wrong' the way the critique says. It is two triggers joined by OR. The miss trigger (5 % of 50 is about 2.5, so 3) is nearly the critique's own rule. The size trigger was never about wording gaps. E-07 justified it by cost and fit: past about 1,000 entries, or about 30k tokens, the one-line index and the agent re-rank of a shortlist stop fitting in a prompt. So 'wording gaps come from description, not size' does not refute the size trigger. It only refutes a reading of it. What does sink the size trigger as an install rule is something the critique did not name: the final design dropped the agent re-rank and the whole-index fallback (KS-R4, §4.1), so the size trigger now has no stated reason. It should become a 'revisit retrieval or recalibrate' checkpoint, not an install trigger.

(b) As written, `v_missed_existing` has no defined writer, so it would almost certainly stay empty. `ks outcome` cannot name an entry, no outcome kind is missed_existing, and nobody classifies the cause. Here are the paths that could fill it:
1. The Jaccard check at record time. It does detect that an entry existed. It is reached reliably on the escalation path, because a miss leads to escalation, and an escalation meets the recording threshold in §7.3. But it is not linked to the miss's lookup id or claim_seq, and it compares words.
2. The Opus reviewer (§7.4). It is not asked to look for existing entries.
3. Reuse of root_cause_id (§3.2 line 231). It needs the author to find the existing root cause first, and no step tells the author to search for it.
4. `ks eval` leave-one-handle-out. It measures synthetic misses, not real ones.
Proposals B and C had the mechanism and lost it in the merge. The critique's fix (Opus checks at record time) restores it and improves on it, because a judgement is not limited to shared words. It is partly there already (the Jaccard extend-not-sibling rule). It also remains a lower bound: misses in sessions that never record stay invisible.

(c) The doc does not claim keyword search wins unconditionally. §4.4 limits dense retrieval's failure to entity-like tokens, and §6.1 says 'unproven'. But line 163's 'evidence that dense retrieval does not beat BM25 at this scale' overstates the lanes, which found no small-corpus evidence either way. 'It depends on the kind of query' mostly restates §4.4. In this store the query kinds split like this:
- Error text, logs, templates, identifiers, `--prescription` doc references and `--files` paths: exact matching and BM25 are strong, and dense retrieval is weak on these tokens.
- Prose symptom descriptions of silent failures and `--action` phase goals: this is where wording mismatch lives (§3.3 'the agent phrases its plan differently (a miss)'), and the do-not-apply and silent-defect entries (ex3, ex4, ex6) are reached mainly this way. Even there, the `--files` intersection is matched exactly, which softens it.
The doc covers the prose kind only with paraphrases written at record time and action handles, and it never learns from misses. So the kind of query that needs embeddings is real, but small.

(d) I expect the figures to come from the literature on textually dissimilar duplicate bug reports, probably Jahan and Rahman (SANER 2023 and the follow-up work): about 20-23 % of duplicates in Bugzilla/Jira datasets share little wording, and detectors do measurably worse on them. If my recollection is right, that drop hits deep-learning (embedding) detectors too, not only keyword methods, so the 'keyword search finds fewer' attribution needs checking. The setting also differs: human reporters on both sides, no paraphrases on the entry side, trackers holding tens of thousands of reports. Here the entries are written by an agent with several paraphrases and the queries are mostly captured logs. So the figures transfer only to the prose and action queries. Even if they are true, they do not overturn the decision ('embeddings later, behind a measured trigger'). The critique's fix keeps that decision. The figures support three things: the miss trigger is the right kind of trigger, the size trigger should be relabelled, and the count must be observable.

(e) Net verdict: partly a slip. The decision stands. The trigger's wording, its reasons and how it gets measured do not. The single most important repair is to define how `v_missed_existing` gets filled, which is the critique's fix in modified form. Without it, D16's miss trigger is decorative.
result.recommended_change:
1. D16 (line 704) and E-07 (line 163). Restate the trigger as at least 3 `missed_existing` lookups classified `vocabulary` (not typo, not handle gap) since the last owner review. A miss whose missed wording was later added as a handle still counts. Stating the class carries KS-A3's adopted graft into D16. Drop 'more than about 1,000 entries' as an install trigger. Re-label it 'past ~1,000 entries, recalibrate thresholds and revisit retrieval', and state its reason honestly: the fit and cost of the index in a prompt, which v1 does not use. Installing anything still needs an owner decision (D5).

2. Define how `v_missed_existing` gets filled, in §7.1, §7.3 and §3.6. `ks record` takes the `--lookup <id>` / `--claim <seq>` of the miss that started the solve; the escalation brief already carries the lookup id (line 435). The write gate's near-duplicate step lists entries that existed at that lookup's time. It matches them three ways: (a) Jaccard; (b) shared `tmpl` or `ident` handles, fix-diff paths that intersect a footprint (the §3.7 join), or the same `root_cause_id`; (c) the Opus author's ruling of same, related or new, which the PR's Opus reviewer checks (§7.4). A 'same' ruling writes `outcome(missed_existing, entry=X, lookup=L, cause=typo|vocabulary|handle_gap)`. Classify typo by edit distance of 2 or less to an entry term, as in proposal C. Classify handle gap as 'a handle kind the query carried was absent on X'. Everything else is vocabulary. The same ruling also writes a `proposed_handle` from the missed query, as in proposal B, so the wording is fixed on the document side before embeddings are considered. Add `missed_existing` to the outcome kinds in §3.6 and an `--entry` option to `ks outcome`.

3. §4.4 (line 313) and line 163. Change 'evidence that dense retrieval does not beat BM25 at this scale' to 'no evidence that dense retrieval beats BM25 at this scale; it underperforms on entity-like tokens (BEIR out-of-domain, Sciavolino); LIMIT is a stress test'. State the split by query kind explicitly. Error, log, identifier and doc-reference queries are lexical. Prose symptom and `--action` queries carry the wording risk; they are served by paraphrases written at record time, action handles and handles derived from misses.

claims.claim: (4) A pattern like compare_digest($$$) does not match text inside comments or string literals, because patterns match AST nodes. This is the critique's 'it never matches inside comments or strings'.
claims.what_sources_say: The pattern-syntax page says 'ast-grep uses pattern code to construct AST tree and match that against target code' and that pattern code 'must be valid code that tree-sitter can parse'. Its worked example says console.log(123) in a comment 'is not matched', and the same for console.log(123) inside a string literal. $META is 'a wildcard expression that can match any single AST node', 'not textual', and $$$ matches 'zero or more AST nodes'. The core-concepts page says tree-sitter is used 'due to its popularity, performance and robustness'. The page defines 'smart' (the default) as matching all pattern nodes while skipping unnamed nodes in the target. It lists comments as ignored only at 'relaxed' and 'signature' strictness. The docs state no general rule that comments and strings are never matched. They show it by example. Caveats from the docs' own wording (my inferences, not run): (a) the 'regex' rule searches a node's full text, so a regex on a node that contains a comment does see it; (b) at the default smart level comments are named nodes and are not skipped, so a comment inside a call's argument list could make a fixed-arity pattern miss (a false absent), while $$$ would absorb it; (c) a string pattern or a string-content probe still matches string nodes by design; (d) code embedded in a string (SQL in a Python string) is opaque to the host-language parse. The critique's second bullet is also right: structural patterns match one syntactic shape and say nothing about the same behaviour written another way.

'off' means never sent, set with --metrics=off or SEMGREP_SEND_METRICS. The design's wording 'ripgrep/ast-grep/Semgrep with metrics off' (design.md line 195) therefore needs the metrics-off qualifier for Semgrep only. claims.claim: (6) tree-sitter recovers from syntax errors with ERROR and MISSING nodes, so a probe on a half-broken file still gets a tree. The implication is that such a probe cannot be treated as authoritative.
claims.what_sources_say: The tree-sitter intro lists as a design goal 'Robust enough to provide useful results even in the presence of syntax errors'. The queries doc says 'When the parser encounters text it does not recognize, it represents this node as (ERROR) in the syntax tree'. MISSING nodes 'appear as seemingly normal nodes in the tree, but they are zero tokens wide', and 'these missing nodes are not captured by (ERROR) queries'. api.h says 'Missing nodes are inserted by the parser in order to recover from certain kinds of syntax errors'; ts_node_has_error is 'a syntax error or contains any syntax errors'. ast-grep's core-concepts page says 'Tree-sitter also handles syntax errors gracefully'. In ast-grep, 'kind: ERROR' matches parse-error nodes (doc comment in kind.rs: 'we can use kind: ERROR in YAML to find invalid syntax'; ERROR is builtin symbol 65535). Implications, as inference: a parse never fails outright. Patterns still match in the intact parts of the file. Inside or next to a broken region the structure may be mis-grouped, so a probe can read a wrong absent, or even a spurious present if the recovered tree resembles the pattern. Neither the ast-grep docs nor the pages I read say what the CLI does or what its exit code is when a scanned file has parse errors. A safe checker should run a 'kind: ERROR' search over the file (or at least over the anchored span) and return inconclusive if it hits. That catches ERROR nodes but not zero-width MISSING nodes, which keep their normal kinds. The napi SgNode exposes no isMissing or hasError.

result.notes:
What the facts mean for the decision (research only; nothing was installed or modified):

1. The critique's ast-grep premise is true as stated. @ast-grep/cli is pinned to exact per-platform packages, including a Windows x64 binary. A Node API (@ast-grep/napi) exists, with a prebuilt Windows .node. Patterns match AST nodes, so text in comments or strings is not matched. The critique's own limit (no parser recognises the same behaviour written another way, so ex3 needs a real test) holds.

2. The facts the critique leaves out:
(a) Language coverage depends on the CLI-versus-napi choice. The design's reader covers Python, TS/JS, JSON, YAML and SQL (design.md line 265). The CLI has the first four built in. The default napi build has only Html, JavaScript, Tsx, Css, TypeScript. For zero-shell-out use from Node, Python, JSON and YAML would each need an @ast-grep/lang-* postinstall package (0.0.x, ISC), which also means another 'install without an owner decision' item.
(b) SQL is not built in either way. @ast-grep/lang-sql 0.0.8 exists, but a Windows prebuild is unconfirmed, and the fallback is 'npm run build', which needs tree-sitter-cli 0.25.8 and a C toolchain. For the CLI route you build a .dll yourself and enable it with --custom-languages (needed since 0.50.0). Also, SQL embedded in Python strings is opaque to the host-language parse.
(c) Windows Defender false-positived the unsigned sg.exe in July 2026 (#2799, #2841). The mitigation, PR #2842, shipped in 0.45.0. Nothing I read says whether 0.51.1 is clean, so test the exact pinned version on the box.
(d) The project is pre-1.0 and run effectively by one maintainer.

3. The README and docs are the source for the language and strictness facts. The strictness default (smart) and the pattern-comment interplay (comments are named nodes, so they may block a fixed-arity pattern, while $$$ absorbs them) are my reading of the docs, not something I ran.

4. Evidence limits: every page was read through WebFetch's summarising model, not raw bytes. npmjs.com package pages returned HTTP 403, so npm facts come from registry.npmjs.org JSON (this includes the 'time' dates, from the tail of a 350 KB document read at an offset). The ast-grep FAQ page 404'd. I could not unpack tarballs (so no direct check of what is inside lang-sql or the win32 packages). I did not run any ast-grep command (the brief forbade install and shell network). Telemetry rests on absence of evidence plus direct dependency lists. The npm cli and napi 'time' values for 0.51.1 differ from each other and from the GitHub release by up to about 8 hours (cli 13:33Z, napi 05:45Z, release 05:33Z), which looks like staged publishing, not a discrepancy that matters. Years for the 25 May to 4 Jul releases are inferred as 2026 from the page ordering and the confirmed 23 Jul 2026 date.

5. Relevant design lines for the reviewer: line 195 ('structural_probe via ripgrep/ast-grep/Semgrep with metrics off' — the metrics-off qualifier applies only to Semgrep), and line 265 (hand-written lexer for Python, TS/JS, JSON, YAML, SQL, with 'ast-grep is the D5 alternative' and a fallback-rate metric KS-9). result.point: Point 2: silent bugs need a code trigger, not a wording match. ex3, ex4 and ex6 have no error text, so lookups driven by errors can never find them, and "a miss is cheap and safe" is wrong for do-not-apply warnings. Proposed fix: when an agent edits a function an entry protects, show that one warning. This breaks the pull-only, no-hooks rule. It is capped at one warning, matched by function, and tested separately in the pilot.

misstatements.critique_claim: Lookups driven by errors can never find ex3, ex4 and ex6.
misstatements.what_doc_says: The design has three non-error triggers built for exactly these entries. (1) The `doc_ref` handle: "this is how an agent about to apply a prescribed fix hits the do-not-apply entry", with ex6 carrying a doc_ref on HANDOFF A2 and §6. (2) The `action` handle: "the only handle for silent defects and predicted hazards with no error text (ex3, ex4, ex6)". (3) §7.2's `--prescription --doc` trigger and the first-commit `ks lookup --files <the Scope paths> --action "<the phase Goal>"`. For ex3 the P12a Scope names AppContext.logPayment and PaymentModal, so the first-commit footprint join would surface it. The real gap is timing and granularity, not "never".
