misstatements.critique_claim: ex6 has no error text.
misstatements.what_doc_says: ex6's symptom does have error text: HTTP 429 with Retry-After on POST /api/auth/login with a correct PIN (R-02 lane line 118). What has no error text is the hazard, an agent about to apply HANDOFF A2's prescription. The design routes that through `--prescription` and `doc_ref`, not through an error lookup.
misstatements.doc_ref: evidence/sweep/lane-R-02.md:118-119; design §3.3 line 254; §7.2 line 437

misstatements.critique_claim: (implied) The doc applies "a miss is cheap and safe" uniformly, with no special treatment for do-not-apply entries.
misstatements.what_doc_says: The global wording is there (§0 rule 1 at line 33, §1.3 at line 89). But the design already treats do_not_apply and open_defect entries asymmetrically in places. Probe-in-lookup never drops them on not_applies (KS-F11). Do-not-apply warning lines are budgeted inside the output cap. A verified do-not-apply hit "stops the change until the phase's Opus reviewer rules". So the slip is that this asymmetry never reached the triggers or the stated principle; it is not wholly absent.

what_critique_gets_right: The asymmetry is real. For a do_not_apply entry or a predicted hazard (ex4 before it fired), a miss is not safe: the agent applies the forbidden change. A spurious warning costs one read, or at worst one Opus ruling. Precision-first tuning and a once-per-phase trigger are the wrong trade-off for this class. §0 rule 1 (line 33) and §1.3 (line 89) state the opposite globally.

The design's only code-anchored trigger has the wrong timing and granularity. It runs once per code phase at the first commit, on the plan's Scope paths. No diff exists yet, so it can only match by file and can never match by function. It does not see what the phase actually edits: mid-phase drift into a protected function, files outside the Scope, and non-phase sessions (KS phases, ad-hoc fixes, workflow subagents) never trigger it. The Scope is prose, not paths: P12a's Scope names `PaymentModal/AppContext.logPayment`, so an agent has to turn it into `--files`.

Function-level matching matters in this repository. Measured with git log -L: backend/app/features/jobs/service.py has 36 commits, but run_dispatch_once (ex4) only 5. src/app/providers/AppContext.jsx has 13, but logPayment (ex3) only 3. backend/app/main.py (ex4's _MAX_DISPATCH_EVENT_AGE at line 94) has 21. A file-level footprint join on these hub files fires on most backend jobs phases, which means alarm fatigue. The 'one cheap join' at first commit is therefore either noisy or pruned.

This is a slip in the adjudication, not only an omission. Judges 2 and 3 both grafted architect B's edit-time `ks guard <paths>` 'before Opus edits in invariant areas' (judge-2.md:162; judge-3.md:159; architect-B.md:358). KS-A4 (line 743) and K23 (line 819) record guard as realised by `lookup --files --action`. But §7.2 and §7.6 schedule that lookup only at the first commit, so the edit-time trigger the judges asked for was lost.

The cited evidence for 'no hooks' does not cover a rare, targeted warning. X-05 F12 and M-02 32 (Gloaguen et al.) measure always-loaded repository context files: over 20% more cost and no general success gain. The same finding says context files are useful 'only for non-standard practices' (lane-M-02.md:139), and a correct-PIN lock is exactly that. M-02's own synthesis rated a hook 'viable' and said the store should be reached 'optionally [through] a hook' (lane-M-02.md:13, :51). M02-02 says the docs point to hooks for must-run behaviour (:79). The owner's own principle (C-01 F52, lane-C-01.md:198) is that 'deterministic code, not the model or a document, enforces rules', with hooks 'local, fast and fail-open'.

HR §4 did not rule out hooks in general. Each skip had a specific reason: the pre-commit verification hook was a blocking git gate with the RT-04/05 defects; the context system was Python, never run live, with undocumented PreCompact behaviour; SessionStart(compact) was skipped because compaction is rare. HR §5's hook objection to Graphify was a hook that nudges every Grep and Read of every agent. A PostToolUse hook that is silent on nearly every edit is not that.
Without any deterministic trigger, compliance stays self-reported (§7.8 line 471; §9 line 538; critic.md:196).
result.reasoning:
(a) The real gap. The design can find ex3, ex4 and ex6 without error text: doc_ref and --prescription for ex6, and the --files/--action first-commit join for ex3 in P12a. The gap is in when and at what grain it does so. The first-commit join runs once, on file paths the plan predicted, before any diff exists. Function-level matching is therefore impossible at that moment, and on hub files the match is noise: jobs/service.py has 36 commits against 5 for run_dispatch_once, and main.py has 21. The --action handle relies on the phase Goal wording matching the solver's phrasing, and the design itself admits a miss (§3.3 line 255). Nothing fires when a phase drifts into a protected function, or when the hazard comes from an agent's own 'obvious fix' rather than a register prescription. The critique's own 'remember this device' scenario is in a new file, so it is caught only by a callers list (point 1), not by matching edits to the protected function. §5.5 (line 349) already lists 'a new caller passing different input to an unchanged function' as undetectable.

(b) What a miss costs. For do_not_apply, open_defect and predicted-hazard entries, a miss forfeits the entry's whole purpose, so 'cheap and safe' is wrong for them. Today the damage is bounded, because the defences are stacked on the existing seeds. ex4 and ex6 are always-loaded CLAUDE.md invariants. They also carry in-code warnings at the exact site: identity/service.py:91-93 ('Deliberately BEFORE verify_pin: a lock has to refuse a correct PIN too'), main.py:90-93, the 0046 downgrade at lines 65-68, and the docstring at tests/test_identity_integration.py:86-92 ('DELIBERATE — do not invert it'). The PR's Opus reviewer, whose brief names register ids, is the last defence. ex3 is weaker. Its code comment at AppContext.jsx:309-310 says a fresh client_id per call 'makes it idempotent so a retry never double-charges', which is the bug itself, so comments are not a reliable warning channel. ex3 also has no protective test, and nothing tests ex4's 0046 seed or age guard (§9 line 514). The harm grows with every lazily seeded do-not-apply entry that has no CLAUDE.md rule behind it. So the critique is right in principle, and the marginal value is small today and grows with the store.

(c) The hook.
(i) Rationale. The doc's stated reason for no hooks, the AGENTS.md study, is about always-loaded context. It does not cover a warning that is silent on nearly every edit. HR §4's skips were specific to their machinery.
(ii) Cost. I measured Node 24.22.1 cold start with node:sqlite at about 90 ms. git calls from Git Bash take about 75 ms each. An in-process span hash against the stored trace on a read-only index connection costs about 100-200 ms per Edit/Write, zero tokens when silent, and about 100-150 tokens when it fires. At this scale (tens of entries, a handful protecting spans), it fires a few times across the whole program.
(iii) Mechanics, from code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks. PostToolUse hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext is 'added to Claude's context alongside the tool result'; plain stdout is not. The hook fires for subagent tool calls, carrying agent_id and agent_type. On Windows it runs under Git Bash, or PowerShell when Git Bash is missing. Write input carries file_path and content; Edit carries file_path, old_string and new_string; file_path is absolute with backslashes. The docs also say the hook does not run for an Edit|Write matcher 'when a Bash command or a process outside Claude Code rewrites the same file'; bashEditDiff is a public beta. That is a material hole here. C-01 F05 found the owner's sessions use the shell tool heavily, and this very session's harness instructions in bypass mode direct agents to edit files with sed and heredocs through Bash.
(iv) Clinic defects. RT-07/09: the absolute backslash path must be normalised to repo-relative POSIX against the worktree root. F50: invoke as `node tools/ks/hook.mjs` so no exec bit is needed. F37 and RT-04: the hook must never block (no exit 2, no decision:block) and never act as proof. The gate stays `ks verify`. F45: dedupe per (session_id, agent_id, entry_id). RT-04's objection to working-tree bytes does not apply to an advisory edit warning, because the working tree is the right input there.
Net: the hook is buildable, cheap and consistent with the owner's fail-open principle. But it is a persistent configuration change, which needs an owner decision (D20's settings.json deny rule is the precedent). It also misses shell edits, so it cannot be the safety backstop.

(d) Hook-free alternative: a diff-time check, `ks lookup --diff <merge-base>`. It reads `git diff --name-only` plus the working tree, recomputes the symbol_span digests already stored in footprints (§3.5), and, with point 1, a one-hop callers list. It runs when the session marks the PR ready (the same moment as `ks record`), and the Opus reviewer runs it as a named step. It catches every change that reaches the PR, whatever tool made it: Edit, Bash, PowerShell or a human. It matches the actual diff, not the plan, at function grain. It changes no configuration and keeps pull-only true. Because the reviewer step is mandatory and SHA-bound, compliance stops being purely self-reported. Its weakness is lateness: a forbidden change can be fully built, tests inverted, before the warning appears. That costs rework, not a merge. The hook's only unique gain is earliness, in sessions that edit through Edit/Write. Chaining the check into each commit's Bash call (as refuter KS-C9 ops suggested for the first-commit lookup) is a middle option.

(e) Verdict. The critique is right that there is a slip. It sits in three places: the global 'a miss is cheap and safe', a trigger that is file-grained, plan-based and fires once, and the dropped edit-time guard graft. Its premise overstates it ('never'; ex6 'no error text'). For this owner, the right fix is the diff-time check plus recall-first rules for do_not_apply and open_defect entries. The hook should be an owner option with default off, decided on measured evidence: an offline replay of historical diffs through the same matcher, and the observed rework from late catches. It should not be adopted by argument now.

(a) The design admits the gap: §5.5 L349, plus §5.2 L337 and §9 L508. It was a deliberate scope line, not an oversight. Lane E-08 f27 says to keep the code call graph out of the store, and §1.4 L109 says the same. The design also already handles known callers by hand: ex3's caller-span precondition (§3.4 L269, KS-F8), and the HANDOFF §6 'visit every caller' shape as a reviewer checklist (§8 rule 6).

(b) The ex6 walk. The PIN check is `verify_pin` in identity/security.py. The lockout check is `throttle.is_locked`, called only inside `IdentityService.login` at service.py:94, deliberately before verify_pin at :97. ex6 is a do_not_apply entry. Its footprint is the login path from f3dfa6f: service.py, throttle.py, repository.py, unlock_account.py and the tests, not security.py. Its protective tests assert that five wrong PINs followed by the right PIN give 429 with Retry-After of at least 1, on POST /api/auth/login, and AccountLockedError from service.login. A device-login endpoint that calls verify_pin and clears the lock is exercised by neither test.

A strict callers list of ex6's own functions would not move. Only an author-chosen guarded identifier would: verify_pin, or references to failed_attempts/locked_until. Even then, §5.2 routes the change to 'suspect'. The next verify re-applies the login mutant, which still flips, the preconditions hold, and the protective test passes. ex6 is reaffirmed and the trace absorbs the new caller. The result is one 'newly suspect' count, printed by `ks close` against origin/main after the merge (L336, L443). It catches nothing.

'Suspect' is also the wrong state. It demotes the warning, capping it at candidate, at exactly the moment its relevance has gone up. The entry is not stale. The code broke the rule, and the check no longer covers every path that verifies a PIN.

(c) Cost is not the obstacle. `git grep -w` per symbol, or one batched call, takes about 60 ms at origin/main. The design's code-token lexer is still needed. Its own KS-3 fixture list includes the comment at identity/service.py:91, which quotes verify_pin and would otherwise be counted as a false caller. Two alternatives are worse here. Python ast needs the off-PATH interpreter. A type-resolving TS call graph would likely miss `app.logPayment(...)` (JobDetail.jsx:680), which goes through the context object; a name search finds it. ast-grep is the D5 install. A name search is not the call-graph tooling HR §5 skipped.

(d) The hub argument holds for transitive closure. But 'one hop' is not a sufficient bound at file level: 22 of the 111 files under src/ already mention AppContext. The bound has to be name references to a few named symbols chosen per entry. logPayment, for example, has one call site. §3.3 L253 already treats AppContext.jsx as a busy file. The Facebook figure is not in the design's evidence and was not verified here. It is also a weak analogy: over-selection there costs test runs, here it costs re-verification and reviewer attention.

(e) This is not a slip in the design: the limit is documented and was a deliberate choice. It is a worthwhile, cheap refinement, but not in the form proposed. The incumbents already cover the example's hazard better than a post-merge flag would: CLAUDE.md's always-loaded Security invariant, Opus routing for auth/PIN, and a refute-by-default reviewer. The strongest fix for the example's bug is a repository CI test, not the store: verify_pin may be called only from login, after is_locked. That is the same idea as D17's promotion of trap probes into CI.

what_critique_gets_right: The route for silent hazards is much coarser than the critique's error-driven framing suggests. The pre-action lookup joins the plan's declared Scope paths, not the actual diff (§7.2 L438, §7.6 L459). It runs once per phase and only when those Scope paths intersect a footprint (KS-F16, §12.5 L781). It runs at the first commit, after the first edits, even though KS-A4 (L743) calls it "the pre-edit lookup". This narrows architect B's original edit-time trigger: "before an Opus phase edits auth, PIN/JWT, outbox, money ... `ks guard <paths>`" (panel/architect-B.md read_when).

No check joins the PR's real diff before merge. Later commits, scope drift outside the declared Scope, and edits by subagents are never joined. `ks close` runs at phase close, after the squash merge (§7.3 L443, §5.2 L336), and re-runs only declarative probes. Code-behaviour entries such as ex6 cannot be declarative leads (KS-F7, §3.4 L264).

The `action` handle is matched as exact verb-object tokens plus FTS. Its stated failure mode is "the agent phrases its plan differently (a miss)" (L255), so the only handle for silent entries is the most wording-dependent one. A phase Goal sentence will rarely contain "let correct PIN clear lock". §9 L513 says so: silent failures are found only if the solver wrote paraphrase and action handles.

In absolute terms "cheap and safe" is wrong for do_not_apply and open_defect entries. The cost of a miss is the forbidden change itself: brute-force throttling removed from 4-digit PINs (ex6), a permanent mass-messaging incident (ex4), legitimate second partial payments swallowed (ex3). The precision-first operating point (§1.3, §4.2) is tuned for the 'act on a wrong fix' risk, and the asymmetry flips for prohibition warnings. The design half-knows this: probe-in-lookup never drops a do_not_apply entry (L293), and do-not-apply warnings get dedicated lines inside the cap (L295).

These misses are unmeasured. `v_missed_existing` needs a `lookup.miss` row (L317, L325), but a do_not_apply miss usually means no lookup ran at all. KS-5 replays only "raw original symptoms" (L605), so the pilot never tests the --files/--action and --prescription routes. That supports the critique's ask to test this separately.

The stake rises as the store succeeds. The design's purpose is to stop CLAUDE.md growing (§1.1 L57-60). Future do-not-apply facts recorded lazily (§8 rule 3) will then live only in the store, with no always-loaded backstop. ex4 and ex6 are protected today mostly because CLAUDE.md already states their rules.

The critique states the rule correctly: the design is pull-only with no hooks (§0 L33; §3.1 L221 "No daemon, watcher or git hook exists"; §7.1 L431; §7.8 L471; §9 L528, L538). The evidence cited for that rule is weaker than the rule itself. X-05 F12 and M-02 32 (Gloaguen et al., arXiv 2602.11988) measure always-loaded repository context files (AGENTS.md), which raised cost by more than 20% without general gains, and M02-32 adds that such files help only for non-standard practices. A rare, targeted do-not-apply warning is that case. The M-02 lane itself rated a hook trigger "viable" and recommended "optionally a hook" (lane-M-02.md L11, L13, L51), and M02-02 notes the docs point to hooks for must-run behaviour. The only hook the panel considered and rejected was a PostToolUseFailure error-injection hook (architect-B and architect-D read_when). HR §4 skipped a pre-commit verification hook for RT-04/05 and the clinic context system (never run live, Python, undocumented behaviour), and HR-C5 kept a SessionStart hook as deferred exact text. Nothing rules out a targeted edit-warning hook in principle.
result.reasoning:
Premises, one by one:
(a) "Error-driven lookups can never find them" misdescribes the document. The design built three non-error routes for exactly ex3, ex4 and ex6: `action`, `doc_ref`/--prescription, and the --files --action pre-action lookup. The real gap is granularity and timing. The pre-action lookup joins the plan's Scope paths, not the diff. It runs once, at the first commit, which is after editing has started even though KS-A4 calls it pre-edit, and only when those paths intersect a footprint. Matching is file-level ident plus wording-dependent action tokens. Nothing joins the PR's actual diff before merge. ks close runs after the merge and re-runs only declarative probes. A mid-phase edit of a protected function, made outside the declared Scope or in a phase whose Goal is worded differently, is never matched.
(b) "Cheap and safe" is accurate as a quote. It holds relative to having no store and fails in absolute terms for do_not_apply and open_defect entries. Today's defences for the three examples are CLAUDE.md's always-loaded rules (ex4, ex6), the D12 correction of HANDOFF A2, ex6's CI tests, the Opus reviewer's duty to list removed assertions and changed expected values (SHIP-PLAN L51-55), and P12a's own spec (ex3). The marginal cost of a store miss on these three is therefore modest now. It grows for future do-not-apply facts that by design never enter CLAUDE.md, and such misses are invisible to v_missed_existing.
(c) The hook works mechanically. I checked https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks on 2026-11-03. PreToolUse and PostToolUse both accept hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext, added next to the tool result. Exit-0 stdout for these events goes only to the debug log, so a silent hook costs zero model tokens. Output is capped at 10,000 characters. The hooks fire inside subagents and carry agent_id. Edit input carries file_path, old_string and new_string; Write carries file_path and content. Commands run in Git Bash on Windows.
Material limits I checked:
- The docs say Claude Code \"doesn't run a PostToolUse hook matching Edit|Write when a Bash command ... rewrites the same file\". This workflow's own subagent context tells agents in bypass mode to make file changes through Bash. So an Edit|Write hook is blind to a whole route; bashEditDiff (beta, best-effort) and FileChanged only partly cover it.
- RT-07/09: tool_input.file_path is absolute and must be normalised to repo-relative POSIX across worktrees and long paths.
- HR-C5's open risks apply: $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR expansion on Windows, and firing in every subagent.
- Hooks in a project .claude/settings.json are missing from worktrees cut from older branches such as release/drain, the same skew §9 L516 names.
- The Compliance Trap (M02-31) applies to warnings too: a false function match can make an agent refuse a legitimate edit.
- Installing the hook is an owner decision (persistent configuration).
Cost per edit is inferred and unmeasured: one Node start plus an indexed SQLite join and a span hash on the edited file, roughly 100-300 ms of wall time and zero tokens when silent. RT-04 does not apply to a warning hook, which proves nothing; it does apply to any commit-time variant, which must read staged blobs.
(d) A hook-free diff-time check closes most of the gap and stays pull-only. It joins the real changed paths and changed symbol spans between the merge-base and HEAD (or the working tree) against do_not_apply, open_defect and trap footprints. It runs before PR-ready, after any push that follows review, and optionally at each commit. It sees every edit route (Edit, Write, Bash, PowerShell, subagents), scope drift and later commits. It costs nothing per edit, needs no harness configuration, and can be named in the Opus reviewer's verdict next to the head SHA, which makes compliance checkable instead of self-reported (§7.8). Its weakness is timing: it catches the change after it is written but before it merges, so a catch costs rework, not damage. The hook catches earlier, at edit time, and does not depend on compliance, but it misses shell edits and adds configuration.
(e) Net: the critique has found a real slip, but not the one it names, and its fix is not the first one to make. The slip is that the coarse non-error trigger conflicts with KS-A4's \"pre-edit\" label, and that \"a miss is safe\" is used for an entry kind where it is false and unmeasured. Make the diff-time check plus the wording correction the default. Offer the edit-time hook, preferably PreToolUse, fail-open and capped at one warning, as a separate owner-gated pilot arm whose false-positive rate is measured first by replaying history.

2. Close the conflict between §7.2 and KS-A4. Either rename the first-commit lookup (it is not pre-edit), or keep it and add the diff-time check below as the real guard.

result.reasoning:
(a) Is the lexer the only safety gate? No. Here is each defence against a wrong present/absent, and whether a lexer slip gets past it.
1. Probe discipline (KS-F7, l.264). For code-behaviour entries it caps every text probe at candidate, so a slip cannot produce a lead or a withheld fix. Contained, except for wrong evidence.
2. Control pairs (fails_at/passes_at, write time). These catch systematic slips on the probed files. Example: a case-insensitive `^revision` probe that fails to strip docstrings counts each of the 46 'Revision ID:' docstring lines beside the 46 `revision =` assignments in backend/alembic/versions. HEAD would then read PRESENT, the pair would not flip, and the check would be refused. Controls do not catch slips on constructs that appear on the target tree after write time. The refuter said this directly: 'vacuity exists only on the current tree'.
3. Refactor mutants and the comment-injection mutant. These test the lexer on the shapes the author wrote. They are lexer fixtures, not an independent defence, and they miss JSX text, regex inside template literals and embedded SQL.
4. Inject-control at reaffirm (l.268). This catches a false ABSENT at the injection site on the current tree, including a truncated span when the mutant lands in the lost tail. It does not catch a false PRESENT.
5. The post-fix-tree rule (l.266). It turns a false PRESENT into a candidate, but `ks close` then reports it as a false 'regression' (l.336).
6. Preconditions (KS-F8). These are themselves lexer-dependent when written as span hashes or probes (ex3's caller span). A slip weakens them rather than being stopped by them.
7. The unique-anchor rule and inconclusive-on-ambiguity. These catch ambiguous matches, not a wrong unique match.
8. Executable checks (test ids, db_probe) and mechanical outcomes (l.309). Both are lexer-independent, but executable checks need Docker (KS-6, conditional on a KS-5 go), and outcomes catch errors only after the fact.

(b) What a lexer slip can corrupt:
- A lead: only for lexer-read data probes (today ex2a). Also indirectly, through a span precondition on a code-behaviour lead after KS-6b.
- A candidate: yes, through the evidence shown with it. Probe-in-lookup can also drop a true candidate on a false ABSENT, which gives a miss.
- The phase-close report: yes. It can raise a false 'regression' or 'fix not on main', or silently miss a real regression, for lexer-based probes.
- Invalidation: yes. A truncated symbol_span hides edits to the rest of the function, the entry stays trusted, and early cutoff re-stamps it wrongly.

(c) Lexing hazards present in this repository:
- JSX. src/features/ops/components/States.jsx:19 has an apostrophe in JSX text followed by `{error?.message ? `(${error.message})` : ""}`. There are 1,059 `</` occurrences across 65 .jsx files, 195 lines of them in JobDetail.jsx.
- Regex literals inside template substitutions. src/features/attendance/pages/Attendance.jsx:184: `` `"${String(c).replace(/"/g, '""')}"` ``. Also technician-app/.../arrival-job/ArrivalJobWizard.tsx:195.
- Regex after `return` or `!`, and an escaped backslash. technician-app/src/lib/architecture.test.ts:50 and :58 (`/\\/g`).
- Division inside multi-line nested templates. JobDetail.jsx:380 and :433-437.
- Nested templates. LogoutButton.jsx:10, jobsApi.js:13, technician-app JobDetailScreen.tsx:814.
- Python f-strings with nested quotes, including an ex1 footprint file: customer_messaging/service.py:145, notifications/service.py:121, ops/health.py:118. No PEP 701 same-quote nesting exists today.
- Raw and bytes strings containing braces and quotes: core/backup.py:37, customer_messaging/tests/test_service.py:132.
- 451 multi-line `def` signatures, whose annotation colons sit inside the parentheses before the body colon.
- SQL inside Python strings. There are no .sql files at all (git ls-files '*.sql' is empty), but there are 37 op.execute calls in 21 migrations. In 0046_seed_dispatch_cursor.py:55-61 the ex4 guard SQL sits inside a triple-quoted f-string with a `'{_CONSUMER}'` literal, and lines 1-36 of its docstring and 66-74 of its comments quote ex4's root-cause tokens (`last_seq=0`, run_dispatch_once). In 0038_job_payment_amount_guard.py:23-28, VALIDATE CONSTRAINT SQL with `--` comments sits inside a docstring, while the real VALIDATE calls are op.execute arguments (0021:113, 0022:96, and the f-string at 0020:107).
- A contradiction in the design: §3.4 strips all string literals before regex_in_span, which hides exactly this op.execute SQL, yet KS-3 tests 'lower-case SQL' mutants against it.

(d) Zero-dependency is a weak reason for the default. The owner's rule allows asking, and the doc already asks (D5).
- What the hand lexer costs: Opus time in KS-3, which competes with the ship program (K8); a parser for Python, JSX/TSX and YAML that is never complete for code that changes every phase; churn on every lexer fix; and a metric blind to its worst failure.

- Whole-file blobs in the meantime fail in the safe direction. Over-invalidation only caps an entry at candidate until `verify` re-stamps it (§5.2 l.335). At tens of entries that is cheap.

(e) What I expect, for the Research lane to verify:
- ast-grep has built-in Python, JavaScript (JSX included), TypeScript, TSX, JSON and YAML, and no built-in SQL. A custom SQL grammar would need a compiled tree-sitter DLL, which means a C toolchain on Windows: a second install.
- For this repository that hardly matters. With no .sql files, the requirement is 'the string argument of op.execute or text()'. A Python rule gives that structurally, and it excludes docstring SQL such as 0038:23-28 at no cost. A small normaliser can then handle case, `--` and `/* */`, and f-string placeholders.
- Parser failure modes to design for: silent ERROR/MISSING nodes from tree-sitter recovery; byte ranges that shift across grammar upgrades (the safe direction); `regex` rules that still see comments inside a matched node; and the npm package possibly relying on a postinstall script (see the open questions).

(f) Yes, the limit clause matches KS-F7 and KS-C14. Adopting a parser must not relax KS-F7.

result.point: Point 3: the rule for adding embeddings (D16) is wrong. Wording gaps come from how people describe symptoms, not from store size. 19–23% of duplicate bug reports are worded differently, and keyword search finds 10–18 points fewer of them. "Keyword beats embeddings at this scale" is not established; it depends on the kind of query. Proposed fix: make misses visible (when Opus records a new entry, it first checks whether an existing entry should have matched), and add a local embedding model only after 3 or more real wording misses.
result.one_line: The fix is right and it closes a real hole: the design's miss counter has no way to ever get filled. But the reasoning is off. D16's miss rule is already about 3 misses (5% of 50). The size rule was about fitting an index in a prompt, not about wording. And the cited numbers compare BM25 against itself, not keyword search against embeddings, so they give no support for embeddings.
what_is_right: The size arm ("more than about 1,000 entries", D16 line 704) is not a valid install trigger in the final design. The critique reaches the right conclusion, for a different reason (see what is wrong).

"At this scale" is not established. Line 163 says "evidence that dense retrieval does not beat BM25 at this scale", but the design's own lanes found no small-corpus study. E-07 F08 says "No peer-reviewed small-corpus BM25-vs-dense study found". T-03 F10 calls LIMIT "a stress benchmark, not a workload like ours". T-03's own recommendation (line 40) was weaker: "no evidence dense retrieval beats BM25". §6.1 line 381 ("unproven at this scale") has the honest wording; lines 163 and 313 do not.

In practice the misses are invisible. §4.6 (line 325) defines the measure as "a lookup.miss whose later outcome names an entry that existed at lookup time". But `ks outcome` (line 426) accepts only resolved, not_resolved or abandoned, with no entry argument. The outcome kinds (line 280) have no missed_existing. No step assigns the typo / vocabulary / handle-gap classification that §4.5 (line 317) promises. Proposals B and C both had a write path, and it was lost in the merge. architect-B line 188: `ks record`'s near-duplicate check "records outcome missed_existing and a proposed handle". architect-C line 207: set "when a newly recorded entry's exact handles, or a handle-token Jaccard of at least 0.6, match an earlier MISS".

Record time is the right place for the check. An Opus author is already present (§7.3, §7.4). A record costs about 5–10k Opus tokens and is rare (§7.7 line 467). The check runs inside a pull verb, so it needs no hook and no install, and breaks none of the standing constraints. It is not the rejected "LLM judge as retain gate" (T-05, line 145): it measures, it does not gate.

Only wording (vocabulary) misses should count toward embeddings. KS-A3 (line 742) says the design adopted "triggers counted only on cause-classified misses", and judge-3 line 240 endorsed it. D16 (line 704) still counts every "missed, entry existed". Typo misses belong to trigram matching and handle gaps to `proposed_handle`; neither is evidence for embeddings.
A fixed count of about 3 is easier to read than "5% over 50 lookups". The KS-9 checkpoint opens at 20 encounters or 8 weeks (line 659), so a 50-lookup window may never fill.

Query kind does matter, and wording-heavy queries really occur in this repo. For ex3 the only on-screen text is the generic toast "Couldn't record payment — please retry" (src/app/providers/AppContext.jsx:324, verified). Any lookup for the double charge is a prose description. §3.3 line 255 admits the `action` handle misses when "the agent phrases its plan differently", and §9 line 513 admits "Lexical retrieval only".
what_is_wrong_or_overstated: "The rule was wrong" overstates it. D16 has two arms joined by OR. Its miss arm (about 5% of 50 lookups, which is about 2.5) is numerically the critique's own "3 or more". The critique's real additions are measurability and the wording-only restriction, not a new threshold.

"Wording gaps come from how people describe symptoms, not from how big the store is" answers a reason the design never gave. E-07 justified the size arm by fit and cost. lane-E-07 line 43: add dense when "the corpus passes roughly 1,000 entries, or the one-line index no longer fits comfortably (~30k tokens)". That is the point where the no-model fallbacks stop fitting in a prompt: the calling agent re-ranking a lexical shortlist (RankGPT), or reading the whole one-line index. The size arm is still dead, but because KS-R4 (line 719) and §4.1 step 3 (line 294: "no LLM re-ranking inside the store"; at most one lead and one candidate shown) removed what it protected, not because wording gaps ignore size.

The quoted claim "Keyword search beats embeddings at this scale" is stronger than anything the doc says. The doc says "does not beat" (line 163) and "unproven" (line 381). §4.4 (line 313) limits the failure to "entity-like tokens".

"It depends on the kind of query" mostly restates the doc. §4.4 limits the claim to entity-like tokens. §3.3 handles prose with write-time paraphrases (line 252) and silent defects with `action` handles (line 255), and §9 admits the prose gap. It is a fair objection to the unconditional "at this scale" wording, not a refutation.

The numbers do not support embeddings. The 10–18 points is BM25 compared with itself: its Recall-rate@100 on textually similar vs dissimilar duplicates. It is not a keyword-vs-embedding gap. In the same paper, the only embedding-style retriever (LDA+GloVe) scored 34–51 points below BM25 on exactly the dissimilar subset. The 19–23% is a hedged estimate with no method behind it, from public trackers with many human reporters and no write-time paraphrases.

The fix as stated is incomplete in four ways.
(1) Opus at record time sees only misses that lead to a record. §7.3 line 443 records only escalations, two or more failed approaches, or burned builds, and recording is "never part of a phase's Done-when". So the count is a lower bound.
(2) It must be linked to the lookup that missed, or the view still cannot join.
(3) An Opus "should it have matched" ruling is an LLM relevance judgement (M-02 30). That is acceptable only because it measures and opens an owner decision.
(4) A bare "3 ever" with no denominator ratchets toward an install over a long enough time. Report it as k of n at KS-9.
where_the_design_is_weak: v_missed_existing has no specified writer, and its only detector is lexical. Correcting both lenses slightly: it is not structurally impossible. The ingredients exist: a miss leads to `ks claim --lookup`, then escalation with the lookup id (line 435), then `ks record` carrying claim_seq (line 453), then the near-duplicate check extends the existing entry X (line 445). So a view could join them. But no section defines that join, no event names X against the miss, and the detector (exact Jaccard on token shingles, over unstated fields) shares the same wording blind spot that caused the miss. As written, the miss trigger is decorative.

The remedy cannot fix what the trigger counts. Neither the critique nor the doc-fidelity lens names this, and it is the most serious gap. §4.4 (line 313) adds vectors "fused by RRF for ranking only, never for abstention". §4.1 step 4 (line 295) admits a candidate only on coverage ≥ θ_cand or an exact handle. A query that shares no words with the entry has coverage 0 and stays a miss even after embeddings are installed. So D16 counts wording misses, and the specified remedy recovers none of them. Admitting a dense-only candidate would not weaken safety: §4.1 states the zero-acted-false-lead target belongs to the gate, not to abstention.

The size arm is orphaned, but should be relabelled rather than dropped. Here I side with the doc-fidelity lens against the engineering lens. Coverage uses IDF from the prose table's fts5vocab (§4.1 step 4). The thresholds are frozen in KS-4 on about 15 seed entries (§4.2), and §4.2 recalibrates only after an engine or recipe change. Corpus growth shifts IDF and margins, so a size checkpoint is legitimately needed, as a recalibration trigger and not as an install trigger. Line 163 also still cites "the calling agent's own LLM as re-ranker", which KS-R4 superseded.

KS-A3's adopted graft never reached D16. The cause classes in §4.5 have no classifier, and the engineering lens's shortcut ("entry was in the stored top-20, so the class is threshold") is too coarse at this size. At 15–200 entries, the internal top-20 holds almost every entry that shares any query term. Classify by term overlap instead: zero shared terms is vocabulary; partial overlap below θ_cand is threshold or partial vocabulary; edit distance ≤ 2 is typo; a missing handle kind is handle gap.

The evidence sentences overclaim.
- Line 163 / §4.4: "at this scale": no cited study is under about 3.6k documents.
- §4.4 cites LIMIT for the entity-token mechanism, but LIMIT attributes the failure to embedding dimension versus top-k combinations. Its own synonym ablation dropped BM25 by more than 89%, which favours dense on wording mismatch.
- The Sciavolino mapping to error codes is marked inferred in T-03 F11 ("my application, inferred") and stated as fact in §4.4.
- Modern embedders (E5; bge-small at MTEB retrieval 51.68, E-07 F22) beat BM25 on the BEIR average.
- "Write-time paraphrase ... captures most of the vocabulary-mismatch benefit" is unsupported: docT5query is about +1.6% over BM25 on the BEIR average.

The evidence does not cover the silent defects. ex3, ex4 and ex6 have no entity tokens, so the evidence about entity-like tokens does not apply to the queries where wording risk lives. Those defects are reached only by prose and `action` handles (lines 252, 255, 513), and §4.3 makes handles only from confirmed hits and refutes, never from misses. So the same wording misses again.
There is no limit stated that v_missed_existing is a lower bound. Misses in sessions that never record stay invisible and could be read as "no misses" (RT-06's unknown-is-not-zero rule).
result.strongest_counter_to_critique:
The design already holds the critique's rule, and the critique's evidence argues for the design's caution, not against it.
- D16's miss arm is about 2.5 misses (5% of 50) of \"missed, entry existed\".
- §4.5 already defines v_missed_existing with typo / vocabulary / handle-gap classes.
- KS-A3 already adopted counting only cause-classified misses.
- The size arm was never a wording claim: lane-E-07 line 43 ties it to the one-line index fitting in a prompt.
- The cited study (Jahan and Rahman, arXiv 2212.09976) measures BM25 against itself. Its 10–18-point Recall@100 gap is near zero at k=5/10 on Eclipse (37.63 vs 37.50 at k=5) and not significant there (p≈0.29). Its one embedding-style method scored 34–51 points below BM25 on the very differently-worded subset.
- Zhang et al. (TOSEM 2023) found the BM25F-based REP beat deep-learning detectors in 5 of 6 trackers, which pay off only at tens of thousands of reports.
So nothing in the critique shows embeddings would recover a single miss here. Its own fix keeps the design's decision: no embeddings until a measured trigger fires.
result.strongest_counter_to_design:
The measured trigger cannot be measured, and the remedy cannot help even if it fires.
- Nothing in §3.6, §7.1 or §7.3 writes a missed_existing outcome or names the existing entry against the lookup that missed.
- The only detector (exact Jaccard on token shingles) is blind in the same way as the BM25 that missed.
- The cause classification KS-A3 claims was adopted has no owner and is missing from D16.
- Even if the count filled, §4.4 adds vectors \"for ranking only, never for abstention\", and §4.1 step 4 requires lexical coverage or an exact handle for a candidate. A zero-overlap symptom (an ex3-style double charge described in prose) stays a miss with embeddings installed.
So D16 is \"never\" in effect, and would be useless if forced. The \"at this scale\" evidence behind the deferral is itself borrowed from large-corpus and stress benchmarks: no study under about 3.6k documents, and LIMIT misattributed to entity tokens. The deferral may well be right, but the design cannot currently tell whether it is.
result.recommended_action:
One amendment, touching D16 and the measurement path, with no change to the install defaults: D5 and D16 still install nothing without an owner decision.

(1) §3.6, §7.1, §7.3: give v_missed_existing a write path.
- `ks record` takes the `--lookup`/claim_seq of the miss that started the solve (the escalation brief already carries the lookup id, line 435).
- Before creating an entry, the write gate gathers entries that existed at that lookup's time with three detectors that do not all depend on wording: the draft's own handles run as a lookup at the miss's index watermark, the §3.7 join from the fix diff's changed files to existing footprints, and the existing Jaccard check.
- The Opus author rules each one same, related or new; the PR's Opus reviewer re-checks the ruling (§7.4).
- A \"same\" ruling writes `outcome(missed_existing, entry, lookup, cause)` plus a `proposed_handle` from the missed wording.
- Add `missed_existing` to the outcome kinds and `--entry` to `ks outcome`.
- Pre-classify cause mechanically by term overlap: zero shared terms is vocabulary; partial overlap below θ_cand is threshold; edit distance ≤ 2 is typo; a missing handle kind is handle gap. `ks close` reports misses never examined as \"unexamined\", never as zero.

(2) D16 and §4.5: the install decision opens when k ≥ 3 vocabulary-class misses are reported as k of n at KS-9. Re-label \"> ~1,000 entries\" as a threshold-recalibration checkpoint (IDF drift), not an install trigger.

(3) §4.4: if vectors are ever added, a dense-only rank-1 hit with a rank margin may yield a candidate. It is never a lead and is still gated; otherwise the remedy cannot recover what the trigger counts. Also:
- Reword \"at this scale\" (lines 163 and 313) to \"no evidence either way at this scale; lexical is favoured for log, identifier and doc-reference queries; prose and `--action` queries are unmeasured\".
- Drop \"captures most\".
- Mark line 163's LLM re-ranker as superseded by KS-R4.

(4) §9: add that v_missed_existing is a lower bound.
result.cited_numbers_status:
\"19–23% worded differently\": real but weak. It comes from Jahan and Rahman, \"Towards Understanding the Impacts of Textual Dissimilarity on Duplicate Bug Report Detection\" (arXiv 2212.09976, SANER 2023), Introduction. It is a hedged, one-sentence estimate (\"could be textually dissimilar\") with no method and no per-dataset breakdown. The paper's working definition of \"dissimilar\" is the bottom quartile by n-gram cosine, so 25% by construction. The closest primary measurement is Chaparro et al. (ICSME 2016), on duplicate pairs with zero shared terms: 33.6% using titles, 19.0% using descriptions, and only 5.1% using title plus description. Both come from public trackers with many human reporters and no write-time paraphrases.

\"Keyword search finds 10–18 points fewer of them\": accurate as literally worded, misleading as used. These are BM25's Recall-rate@100 gaps between textually similar and dissimilar duplicates: Eclipse 10.20, Firefox 10.86, Mobile 18.45. They are not a keyword-vs-embedding gap. The gap is near zero at k=5/10 on Eclipse and not significant there (p≈0.29). The dissimilar set is defined lexically, which makes the gap partly circular. The only embedding-style method in the paper (LDA+GloVe) scored 18.5 / 8.0 / 15.0 on that subset against BM25's 52.6 / 46.7 / 59.6. Read as evidence for embeddings, the figures are contradicted by their own source. (One research note attributed 2212.09976 to \"Zhang et al.\"; the authors are Jahan and Rahman. Zhang et al., TOSEM 2023, is a separate paper that found the BM25F-based REP best in 5 of 6 trackers.)

\"3 or more\": the critique's own parameter, not from the literature; it matches D16's 5% of 50 ≈ 2.5.

The design's own numbers: the D16 / E-07 trigger values are marked inferred owner parameters (line 163, KS-R10 line 725). The \"at this scale\" claim rests on BEIR (corpora of 3.6k to 15M documents) and LIMIT (a synthetic stress test). The literature figures were read from extracted PDF text or through a summariser.

result.point: Point 1: add a one-hop "who calls this function" list to each entry's footprint. The example is a later "remember this device" login in a new file that calls the PIN check and clears the lock without the lockout check. That would turn ex6 suspect instead of leaving it trusted. The list stops at one hop because hubs like AppContext.jsx flag everything, citing Facebook's transitive test selection: about 10,000 tests, 99.9% of which passed.
result.one_line: The gap is real and cheap to close without hooks or installs, but the proposed mechanism misses its own example: verify_pin is not in ex6's footprint, and early cutoff would clear the "suspect" flag anyway. The design names this limit openly, so it is not a slip. The best fix for the example belongs in a CI test, not the store.
what_is_right: The hole exists, and the design admits it in so many words. §5.5 L349 lists among the things it cannot detect: "Semantic changes outside the footprint (a new caller passing different input to an unchanged function)". §5.2 L337 and §9 L508 say "an unchanged footprint is necessary, never sufficient". The wording comes from architect-A.md:214, and the KS-C8 refuter named the same hole.

On today's tree the example really is invisible. verify_pin has one non-test caller, service.py:97, checked at origin/main. The lock-state writers are service.py:88-89/100-101/107-108/136-137 and scripts/unlock_account.py:83-84. A new file that calls verify_pin and writes failed_attempts/locked_until changes no footprint item, so none of the eleven §5.1 triggers fires (L331). The only pre-merge pull, the first-commit lookup at §7.2 L438, is keyed on Scope paths intersecting a footprint, so a brand-new path can slip past it.

The "second door" shape is real in this repo: HANDOFF §6 item 7 ("a shared contract changed without visiting every caller"), head_size's second caller, and CLAUDE.md's dispatcher note "reopened through the automated door". Identity is also not covered by the import-linter independence contract, so any slice can import identity.security.verify_pin.
One hop is the right bound if callers are computed at all. Transitive or import closure through AppContext.jsx is unusable: about 22 of 111 src files mention it.

It is cheap, needs no install and stays pull-only. A batched `git grep -w` for about 11 symbols over origin/main measured 60-100 ms on this box. Distinctive guarded functions have tiny caller sets: verify_pin 1, create_access_token 1, compare_secret 3, logPayment 1, run_dispatch_once 1. Point 1 does not need point 2's hook.

It does not conflict with HR §5 in substance. HR skipped graphify, a persistent graph with a PreToolUse hook and a day-old package. The same review says "the hot-path call sets are small enough for grep" (HR Q3 L48) and uses grep/ast-grep as ground truth for callers (§5 L300).
what_is_wrong_or_overstated: A callers list of ex6's own footprint misses the critique's own example. ex6's fix_diff tier (§3.5 L276; `git diff --name-only`, fix 1c546a3/f3dfa6f) covers repository.py, service.py, throttle.py, scripts/unlock_account.py and tests, not security.py. verify_pin appears in the fix only inside an added comment ("Deliberately BEFORE verify_pin", service.py:91), and KS-F7 strips comments (L265). The new code calls verify_pin and, by definition, skips is_locked. So the callers of login, the throttle functions and get_for_update do not change. "Suspect" is the wrong state anyway. ex6's claim is still true: login refuses a correct PIN while locked. The new code is a fresh violation of the rule through a path the protective test does not cover. Marking the entry suspect caps it at candidate (L293) at the moment it matters most.
"Today ex6 stays trusted" is inaccurate. ex6 is seeded `unverified_seed`, which is candidate-only, until KS-6/KS-6b (§8 rule 1 L490; §10 KS-4 L594).

Calling it a slip overstates. The limit is documented (§5.5, §9), and known callers are already handled by hand as preconditions (ex3's "the caller span in JobDetail.jsx unchanged", L269/KS-F8). What the design lacks is detection of new callers, not awareness of callers.

The Facebook figures support "transitive closure over-selects". They do not support "one hop is enough": the paper never discusses a one-hop bound, and the other literature (below) treats depth 1 as giving up recall. One hop also does not bound noise at file level: 22 files reach AppContext in one hop. The bound has to be name references to a few named symbols.
where_the_design_is_weak: §1.4 L109 ("Call-graph tooling was evaluated and skipped (HR §5)") rules out more than its source did. HR §5 skipped graphify for tool-specific reasons and endorsed grep for small call sets. E-08 f27 only says not to store a call graph in the store. Neither forbids an on-demand name search. As a result, §5.5 L349 files as undetectable a case that a 0.1 s git grep can detect: a new reference to a guarded identifier.

The design has no identifier-keyed, pre-merge pull. The first-commit lookup (L438) keys on Scope paths. The PR's Opus reviewer refutes recorded entries (L449, L461) but never runs a lookup over the diff's newly referenced identifiers. Every footprint signal otherwise reaches origin/main after the merge, at `ks close` (L336).

A dangling flag: L293 routes `--touching` identifier queries to the `ident` handle, but the CLI surface (L423) and the KS-2 scope (L572) list only --files, with no --touching. That missing flag is exactly where this feature would live.

Early cutoff (L335) re-stamps any changed trace item whose controls still flip. Any coverage-gap signal routed through suspect is therefore self-clearing by construction. The design should say plainly that footprint drift never means "the rule now has an uncovered site".
result.strongest_counter_to_critique: Two reasons the store is the wrong place for this catch. First, the realistic version of the example is caught better elsewhere, and earlier. In this repo's slice layout (router → service → repository), a device login almost certainly edits identity/service.py. That file's blob is already in ex6's footprint, and the phase's Scope would trigger the first-commit lookup (L438) before any code is written. For the narrow residual case, a new file only, a backend pytest that uses stdlib ast to pin the closed caller sets of verify_pin and create_access_token to IdentityService.login fails in CI before the merge, for every agent and human, with no store involved. A device login has to mint a JWT through create_access_token even if it skips verify_pin. That is the design's own D17 route (L705), and the same move HR made with dependency-cruiser. Second, a store-side callers list routed to "suspect" would demote the warning, clear itself on reaffirm, and arrive after the merge.
result.strongest_counter_to_design: The design calls a known hole undetectable when it is detectable cheaply, with no hook and no install: a new reference to a guarded identifier, found by git grep at the PR head. It reaches that conclusion by stretching HR §5's graphify skip into a ban on all caller tooling, which HR itself did not make (HR Q3 L48 says grep suffices for these call sets). The result is that a do_not_apply/invariant entry like ex6, whose whole job is to stop a second-door violation, has no pre-merge signal when the door is in a new file.

result.reasoning:
(a) Is the lexer the only safety gate? No. Each defence against a wrong present/absent, and what a lexer slip does to it:
- KS-F7 probe discipline (l.264): blocks the slip for code-behaviour leads. A wrong PRESENT can only become candidate plus evidence.
- Absence-polarity rule (KS-A5 l.744, l.264): blocks it. A wrong 'guard absent' gives inconclusive.
- Post-fix-tree rule (l.266): blocks it.
- Control pairs (l.267): partial. They catch a slip only on the fails_at/passes_at blobs at write time, not one triggered by later code on the current tree.
- Refactor mutants and the comment-injection mutant (l.267): partial. They catch only the slip classes the mutant set exercises (file move, comment edit, rename, YAML quoting, SQL case). JSX text, regex/division and template-nesting slips pass unless golden fixtures add them.
- Inject-control at reaffirm (l.268): catches a slip that makes the probe blind on the current tree (wrong ABSENT near the mutant). It does not catch a wrong PRESENT on the current tree.
- Ambiguous anchor gives inconclusive, unresolved anchor falls back to the whole file (l.265): catches detected failures; silent mis-anchors pass.
- Preconditions (l.269): orthogonal, and can themselves be corrupted when expressed as spans (ex3's JobDetail.jsx caller span).
- Executable checks (test ids, db_probe): immune to the lexer, and they are the code-behaviour gate.
- Outcome events (§4.3 l.309): catch a wrong lead after acting.
- 'Gate always runs' (l.337): staleness errors cannot cause an action by themselves.
So the lexer is not on the lead path for code behaviour at all, and the main premise is wrong.

(b) What a slip can actually corrupt:
- A lead: only through data-value probes that are not JSON: ex2a's duplicate_values over Python (its interaction with string stripping is unspecified) and any future YAML or Python config trap. ex7 and ex8 use JSON.parse.
- A candidate's shown probe evidence: yes, including ex1's symbol-scoped compare_secret exclusion.
- The phase-close report (§5.2 l.336): yes, if a validated entry's probe is a lexed text probe. That means false 'regression' noise or a missed regression. ex4 is the one CI does not cover; its probe reads SQL inside a Python string, which string-stripping erases.
- Invalidation: yes. A span cut short by a mis-matched brace hides a later edit (missed suspect). A desync caused by unrelated code above the span gives a spurious suspect, which is the safe direction. Neither acts without the gate.

(c) Hazards: concrete and numerous; each is listed with file:line in what_critique_gets_right. The design's own anchor files are exposed: AppContext.jsx:229, above the ex3 span. JobDetail.jsx is JSX-heavy, and the spec does not mention JSX.

(d) Zero-dependency as the reason for the default: defensible but weak. The owner rule is 'nothing without an owner decision', and D5 already asks. KS-3 cannot start before D1b, so bundling a D5 'ast-grep yes' into that same ruling adds no owner touchpoint. On the other side of the scale are four hand lexers that Opus must build and maintain, never evaluated, measured only at KS-9. Also left unconsidered by §3.4 are real parsers already on the box with no new install: TypeScript 5.3.3 in technician-app/node_modules, and @babel/parser 7.29.7 and acorn 8.16.0 in root node_modules. They are app-owned, though, and absent in worktrees without node_modules. Python's `ast` is not available, because python3 is a WindowsApps stub. Since the lexer is not the lead gate, the case for a parser is about quality (evidence, scan precision, span stability, the ex2a/YAML data-value route), not about closing an acted-false-positive hole.

(e) Language coverage. I expect ast-grep built-ins to include Python, JavaScript (with JSX), TypeScript, TSX, JSON and YAML, and SQL not to be built in (custom languages need a compiled tree-sitter dynamic library, a further native install on Windows). If SQL is missing, little is lost here: every SQL fragment is a Python string argument of op.execute or sa.text. ast-grep can locate those string nodes structurally and apply a case-insensitive regex to their content. That covers the SQL-case mutant, ex4 and ex2c without a SQL grammar. SQL `--` comments inside those strings would still need a regex rule. The hand lexer has the same embedded-SQL gap, and a worse one, because it strips the strings.

(f) The limit clause agrees with KS-F7/KS-C14/KS-C11 and with §3.4 l.272. It also undercuts the headline: because the doc already refuses text-probe leads for code behaviour, swapping in a parser does not change the safety gate for ex1 or ex3-ex6. Two further caveats: 'never matches inside comments or strings' holds for ast-grep pattern rules but not for regex rules, and tree-sitter recovers from errors silently (ERROR nodes), so a parser can also slip unless ERROR inside an anchored span maps to inconclusive.
result.recommended_change:
Keep the probe discipline as written, and correct the critique's framing: the lexer is the evidence, span and scan engine, not the lead gate. Then make these changes.
1. In D5, recommend ast-grep (pinned exact version, invoked through execFileSync with --json, like git) as the default answer for the span anchor and code-token matcher. Rule it together with D1b, so no extra touchpoint is added. Keep the hand lexer only as the fallback if the owner declines. Note in §3.4 that the TypeScript compiler API and @babel/parser are already present (app-owned) as a no-new-install alternative for JS/TS, with the worktree node_modules caveat.
2. In §3.4, define three reading modes:
   - code tokens: comments and strings stripped, for regex/ordered/count probes;
   - code plus string values, comments stripped, for duplicate_values and Python or YAML data-value extraction, such as ex2a's `revision: str = \"0046\"`;
   - embedded SQL: the string argument of op.execute or sa.text, re-read as SQL with `--` and `/* */` stripped and keywords compared case-insensitively. This covers ex4's 0046:57 seed and the KS-3 lower-case-SQL mutant.
3. State that a YAML or Python data value is lead-capable only when read by a real parser. Under the hand lexer it caps at candidate.
4. Map lexer desync, or a parser ERROR node inside an anchored span, to inconclusive.
5. Add golden fixtures taken from the repo's real hazards: AppContext.jsx:229, Attendance.jsx:184, LogoutButton.jsx:10, ApiMetrics.jsx:100, JobDetail.jsx:352, customer_messaging/service.py:75, 0046:56-61, deploy.yml:71-76, dependabot.yml:34-43.
6. Measure silent mis-lexes as well as unresolved anchors. Run a whole-repo differential in KS-3 (hand-lexer spans against a real parser), and report it before KS-5 instead of only at KS-9.
7. Record in §9 that comment stripping fixes one of KS-C14's four fooling modes, and that ex3 still needs P12a's test.

result.point: Point 2: silent bugs need a code trigger, not a wording match. ex3, ex4 and ex6 have no error text, so lookups driven by errors can never find them, and the doc's "a miss is cheap and safe" is wrong for "don't do this" warnings. Proposed fix: when an agent edits a function an entry protects, show that one warning. This breaks the pull-only, no-hooks rule. It would be capped at one warning, matched by function, and tested separately in the pilot.
result.one_line: You are right that the design has a real gap for "don't do this" entries and that "a miss is safe" is false for them. You are wrong that the doc only uses error-driven lookups, and the first fix should be a check on the PR's diff, which needs no hook. The edit-time hook should be a later owner option, off by default.
what_is_right: "A miss is cheap and safe" is false for do_not_apply and open_defect entries. The text is §0 rule 1 (L33, "A miss costs nothing and changes nothing"), §1.3 (L89) and the "(safe)" labels at L252 and L256. For a prohibition entry, a miss lets the forbidden change through: brute-force throttling removed from 4-digit PINs (ex6), a permanent mass message (ex4), a legitimate second partial payment swallowed (ex3). The precision-first setting (§1.3, §4.2) suits the risk of acting on a wrong fix, and the trade-off reverses for these kinds. The design half-knows this already: probe-in-lookup never drops these kinds (L293), and warning lines get room inside the output cap (L295).

The only code-anchored trigger for silent hazards is coarse. §7.2 L438 runs `ks lookup --files <the Scope paths> --action "<the phase Goal>"` once per phase, at the first commit, and only when those predicted paths intersect a footprint. It joins the plan's Scope, not what was actually edited. The first commit is also when the draft PR opens (SHIP-PLAN L31), so in a one-PR phase like P12a it can be the whole change. Nothing joins the PR's real diff before merge. `ks close` runs after the merge and re-runs only declarative probes (L336), and code-behaviour entries cannot use those (KS-F7, L264).

Matching by function matters in this repo. I re-counted on this branch: backend/app/features/jobs/service.py has 36 commits, but run_dispatch_once (ex4) only 5. AppContext.jsx has 13, but logPayment (ex3) only 3. main.py, which holds ex4's age guard, has 21. A file-level join on these shared files would fire on most phases that touch them.

The design itself slipped here. Architect B's edit-time `ks guard <paths>` ("before an Opus phase edits auth, PIN/JWT, outbox, money...", architect-B.md L358) was adopted by judge 2 (L162) and judge 3 (L159). KS-A4 (L743) and K23 (L819) record it as "realised as `ks lookup --files --action`" and still call it "the pre-edit lookup". §7.2 then schedules that lookup at the first commit, which drops the edit-time property the judges asked for.

§5.2 (L335) reads a protected span changing in the working tree as "suspect for this caller only", meaning the entry may be stale. For a do_not_apply entry, that change is exactly the event the entry exists to catch. The data needed to match by function is already there: `symbol_span` footprint items (§3.5 L276), and the changed-path join in §3.7 L286.

"Tested separately in the pilot" is warranted. KS-5 writes blind queries only "from raw original symptoms" (L605), so the --files/--action, --prescription and diff routes never get measured. `v_missed_existing` (L317, L325) needs a `lookup.miss` row, and a do_not_apply miss usually means no lookup ran at all, so these misses are invisible.

The critique is right to treat the hook as an owner decision. It is also right that the doc's "no hooks" rule rests on weaker evidence than it implies. §7.1 L431 cites X-05 F12 and M-02 32 (Gloaguen et al.), which measured always-loaded context files and found them useful "only for non-standard practices" (lane-M-02 L139). The M-02 lane itself rated a hook "viable" (L13) and suggested "optionally a hook" (L51). The only hook the panel rejected was a PostToolUseFailure error-injection hook (architect-B L358). HR §4's skips were each for specific reasons (the pre-commit hook for RT-04/05, the context system as never run live; the SessionStart(compact) hook was only deferred). None of them is a blanket ban.
what_is_wrong_or_overstated: "Lookups driven by errors can never find them" misdescribes the doc. Three non-error routes are built for exactly these entries. The `action` handle is described as "the only handle for silent defects and predicted hazards with no error text (ex3, ex4, ex6)" (§3.3 L255). `doc_ref` plus `--prescription --doc` is "how an agent about to apply a prescribed fix hits the do-not-apply entry" (L254, §7.2 L437, which names ex6). Third is the first-commit `--files --action` lookup (L438). For ex3, P12a's Scope names `PaymentModal/AppContext.logPayment` (SHIP-PLAN L656-664), so that route reaches it in the very phase that fixes it. The error-only framing is true only of the front-page diagram (§0 L17) and §1.5 L117.

"ex3, ex4 and ex6 have no error text" holds only partly. The doc groups them that way itself (L255), so the critique followed the doc. But ex6's symptom is "HTTP 429 with Retry-After on POST /api/auth/login even though the PIN is correct" (lane-R-02 L118). An agent who sees it and goes to "fix" it reaches the store through the error route (§7.2 L439). ex3 shows a failure toast. ex4 never fired.

"A code trigger, not a wording match" is a false choice. ex4's real trigger is an operator action outside git: setting FIXFLOW_ENABLE_DISPATCHER=true on Railway, resetting the cursor by hand, or restoring an older snapshot (lane-R-02 ex4). No edit hook and no diff check can see any of that. Only the wording-based `action` handle ("enable dispatcher", L255) reaches it. Code-edit hazards need the code trigger, and operator-action hazards still need the wording match.

The doc does not apply "a miss is safe" with no exceptions. Relative to having no store, it is literally true: the agent proceeds as it does today. For the three named entries the extra harm from a miss today is small, because each sits behind several layers. CLAUDE.md always loads the login-lock and dispatcher rules, and §8 L500 keeps every rule sentence. There are in-code warnings at the exact sites: identity/service.py L91-93, the test docstring "DELIBERATE — do not invert it" (test_identity_integration.py L86-92), the deliberate no-op in 0046's downgrade (L64-68) and main.py L90-93. The Opus reviewer must list every removed assertion and changed expected value (SHIP-PLAN L51-55). P12a's own scope prescribes rotate-on-success-or-change. One correction: ex3's in-code comment (AppContext.jsx L309-310) claims idempotency and is itself wrong, so comments are not a dependable warning channel.

An edit-time hook is not the right first mechanism. An Edit|Write hook does not fire when Bash or PowerShell rewrites the file (per the hooks docs, as both lenses read them), and this workflow's own subagent context tells agents in bypass mode to make file changes with sed and heredocs through Bash, which I saw in my own instructions. So the hook is blind to a whole edit route and cannot be the safety backstop. It is also persistent configuration (D20 is the precedent for an owner gate). And a spurious warning pushed to a cheap agent is not free: the Compliance Trap paper (M02-31) shows agents adopt the first memory they are shown.
where_the_design_is_weak: No step joins the PR's actual diff, at function grain, against do_not_apply, open_defect and trap footprints before merge. Scope drift, later commits, edits by subagents and edits through Bash are never matched.

The `action` handle, the only route for operator-action hazards, depends on wording. The doc admits its failure mode is "the agent phrases its plan differently (a miss)" (L255), and §9 L513 says silent failures are found only if the solver wrote paraphrase and action handles.
KS-A4 calls the first-commit lookup "pre-edit", and §7.2 places it at the first commit. In small phases that is after the edits.
§5.2 reads a changed protected span as staleness, not as a warning, for prohibition kinds.
The pilot (KS-5 L605) measures only symptom replays. Misses on prohibition entries are unmeasured, and §7.8 L471 admits compliance is self-reported.

The stake rises as the store succeeds. §7.3 L443 records do-not-apply facts in the store, the doc's aim is to stop CLAUDE.md growing (L57), and lazy seeding (§8 rule 3) means future do-not-apply facts drawn from HANDOFF, G2 or W2 notes may live only in the store, with no always-loaded rule behind them.

Function-level matching depends on the anchoring choice. With the hand lexer, an unresolved anchor falls back to the whole file (L276), which brings back noise on shared files. This links point 2 to the critique's preamble about the reader (D5, ast-grep).
§7.1 L431 and §9 L528 cite X-05 F12 and M-02 32 as a blanket "no hook" rule, but that evidence covers only always-loaded context and error-injection hooks.
result.strongest_counter_to_critique: For the three entries the critique names, the design already has routes that need no error text, and a miss costs almost nothing today. ex6 has error text (a 429 on a correct PIN), a doc_ref on HANDOFF A2, an always-loaded CLAUDE.md rule, a "do not invert" docstring on its protective test, and a reviewer obliged to list removed assertions. ex3 is reached in P12a by the first-commit lookup, and P12a's own spec prescribes the correct rotation. ex4's dangerous moment is mainly an operator action outside git (the dispatcher env flip, a hand cursor reset, a snapshot restore) that no edit or diff trigger can see; only the wording-based `action` handle reaches it. The proposed Edit|Write hook misses Bash and PowerShell edits, which this harness tells agents to prefer in bypass mode, so it cannot be the backstop. Building it before the KS-0 audit also contradicts the design's own rule to build nothing before the pilot that the pilot does not need (§0 L43).
result.strongest_counter_to_design: For silent prohibition entries, the design's only code-anchored trigger is one file-level join, run once, over the plan's predicted Scope paths at the first commit (which in a one-PR phase can be the whole change), plus `action` matching that depends on wording. Nothing joins the real diff before merge. `ks close` runs after the merge and re-runs only probes that code-behaviour entries cannot have. §5.2 files the exact event a do_not_apply entry exists for under staleness. The pilot never tests these routes. The judges' edit-time `ks guard` graft was recorded as adopted but lost its edit-time property. On shared files (jobs/service.py 36 commits against 5 for run_dispatch_once; main.py 21) the file-level join is noisy. And "a miss costs nothing" will turn false in practice once do-not-apply facts live only in the store.
result.recommended_action:
Amend KNOWLEDGE-STORE-DESIGN-2026-11.md before KS-2. Install nothing and add no hook now.
(1) In §0 rule 1, §1.3 L89, and §3.3 L252 and L256, limit "a miss is cheap and safe" to solved entries. For do_not_apply and open_defect entries, make triggers recall-first and say that their misses are measured.
(2) Add a `--diff <merge-base>` form to `ks lookup` in §7.1 and §7.2, built in KS-2/KS-3 on the existing §3.7 changed-path join. It joins the paths and `symbol_span` hashes that changed between the merge-base and HEAD or the working tree. The comparison is against the diff, not the stored trace, so an unrelated change merged earlier does not keep firing. It covers do_not_apply, open_defect and trap footprints and prints at most one warning card naming the entry and the protected span. Amend §5.2 so that, for these kinds, a hit is a warning, not a staleness label.
(3) Add to the §7.6 Routing sentence: "The reviewer runs `ks lookup --diff <merge-base>` at the PR head SHA and names every do-not-apply warning it printed and how the diff respects it." That makes the check deterministic at the one step that is already mandatory, and it answers §7.8's self-reporting gap.
(4) Correct KS-A4 (L743) and K23 (L819): the first-commit lookup is an early hint, not "pre-edit", and the diff check is what realises the judges' guard. In §3.3 and §9, state that the `action` handle stays the only route for operator-action hazards (ex4's dispatcher flip).
(5) Add a diff arm to KS-5 that runs offline with no hook. Replay the commits on main that touch the seed footprints, plus synthetic forbidden diffs: HANDOFF A2's patch with the two protective tests inverted, a 0046 downgrade that deletes the cursor, and the naive PaymentModal useState. Also include an unrelated AppContext.jsx edit, which must stay silent. Report recall and false fires per phase.
(6) Add D21, default off: a fail-open PreToolUse (or PostToolUse) hook on Edit|Write that calls the same join. Requirements: one warning of at most 300 characters; repo-relative POSIX paths; deduped per session, agent and entry; never blocking. Its stated blind spot is Bash and PowerShell edits. Rule on it at KS-9 only if the replay's false-fire rate is acceptable and late catches showed real rework or reviewers skipped the check.
(7) Reword §7.1 L431 and §9 L528 so the no-hook rule cites what its evidence covers: always-loaded context and error-injection hooks.
