- Node cold start of about 90 ms and a per-edit hook cost of about 100-300 ms are the lens's own measurements and inferences. I did not re-check them.

The critique's figures for the other points, per the research:
- 99.9%: supported. Machalica et al. §III-B says "almost 99.9%" of tests chosen by build dependencies pass.
- ~10,000: the paper's order-of-magnitude phrasing (10^4) in its introduction. Its body says only "much greater than 1000" targets.
- 19-23%: real, but a hedged, unexplained estimate from Jahan and Rahman (arXiv 2212.09976; one research note wrongly credits it to Zhang et al.).
- 10-18 points: BM25's recall@100 gap between similarly and differently worded duplicates (10.20 / 10.86 / 18.45). It is not a keyword-versus-embedding gap, it is near zero at k=5-10, and Eclipse's gap is not significant.

result.point: Point 0 (the header): syntax trees should run the checks. The doc plans a hand-written reader for five languages, those checks are the store's only safety gate, and every slip in that reader becomes a wrong present or absent. ast-grep is a maintained parser (one pinned npm package with a prebuilt Windows binary) that never matches inside comments or strings, which is what fooled the text checks. The limit: no parser recognises the same behaviour written a different way, so ex3 still needs a real test.
result.one_line: You found a real slip: an untested hand-written lexer is scheduled before the pilot. But the reason you give is wrong. Under KS-F7 that lexer never decides a code-behaviour lead, so swapping in ast-grep changes quality, not the safety bound. The better fix is to build neither one before the pilot, then rule on ast-grep at KS-6.
what_is_right: The default really is a hand-written lexer and span anchor (§3.4 l.265; KS-3 Scope l.583; D5 default 'the hand lexer with golden fixtures', l.693). Nobody evaluated it. It was adopted straight from the completeness critic's suggested fix, and the critic itself wrote 'No register lane evaluated a hand-written lexer or parser' and 'a lexer bug yields false PRESENT or ABSENT' (critic.md l.74-77). The design's own register had pointed at real parsers instead: Python ast and the TypeScript compiler API in X-03 (l.197), ast-grep in M-03 and X-02 (l.179, l.195).

'Every slip becomes a wrong present or absent' is true at the level of what a probe reads. Wherever the lexer is the reader, a slip corrupts the result directly: candidate evidence, symbol_span hashes (§3.5 l.276), span preconditions (ex3's JobDetail.jsx caller span, l.269) and the phase-close re-run of validated declarative probes (§5.2 l.336). The phase-close scan can then raise a false 'regression' or miss a real one.

The hazards are concrete in this repo, and the lexer spec does not cover them; I spot-checked these. JSX is never mentioned, yet JobDetail.jsx (a precondition anchor) has 195 lines containing '</', and States.jsx:19 puts an apostrophe in JSX text right before a template literal. AppContext.jsx:229 has a regex literal holding 5 double quotes, directly above the ex3 logPayment span at 312-328. Attendance.jsx:184 puts a regex with a lone quote inside a template substitution. The ex4 guard SQL sits inside a triple-quoted f-string at 0046_seed_dispatch_cursor.py:56-61. The repo has 0 .sql files and 37 op.execute calls across 21 migrations.

The design contradicts itself on SQL. §3.4 strips string literals before regex, ordered and count probes, yet the KS-3 fault list tests a 'lower-case SQL' mutant against SQL that exists only inside Python strings.

The design's only health metric for the lexer, the KS-9 'fallback rate' (l.265, l.660, l.693), counts anchors the lexer knows it failed to resolve. A span that resolves silently to the wrong range is the dangerous case, because it hides an edit and the entry stays trusted, and the metric does not count it. The metric is also read only at KS-9, after the KS-5 go/stop decision.

The ast-grep facts mostly hold (research, registry manifests): @ast-grep/cli is MIT, with exact-pinned per-platform optionalDependencies that include a prebuilt win32-x64-msvc binary. Its postinstall only hard-links that binary and makes no network calls. The CLI has Python, JavaScript (with JSX), TypeScript, TSX, JSON and YAML built in. Pattern rules match AST nodes, so text in comments and strings is not matched.

The limit clause matches the design exactly: KS-F7 (l.264), §9 l.509, KS-C11 (l.783: the correct P12a fix, the naive useState fix and rotate-on-close all leave AppContext.jsx byte-identical) and §3.4 l.272 (ex3 is an open_defect that takes P12a's own test id as its check).
what_is_wrong_or_overstated: 'Those checks are the store's only safety gate' is wrong. KS-F7 (l.264) says that for a code-behaviour entry no text probe of either polarity may return applies; at most it gives candidate plus evidence, and only an executable check can lead. §4.1 l.295 assigns the zero-acted-false-lead target to the gate's preconditions and executable checks. The post-fix-tree rule (l.266) turns a text-probe PRESENT into a candidate. An ABSENT on an open_defect is inconclusive (l.296). Probe-in-lookup never drops an open_defect or do_not_apply entry (l.293). An unchanged footprint is 'necessary, never sufficient' (l.337). Mechanical outcomes and v_gate_wrong come on top (l.309). For ex1 and ex3-ex6 the lexer is not on the lead path at all.

The lead-capable probes mostly do not go through the lexer. ex7 and ex8 read JSON through a real JSON.parse ('JSON: pointers over a parse', l.265), and dep_version reads lockfile JSON. The only lead route a lexer slip can reach today is ex2a's duplicate_values over Python. Its systematic slips are caught at write time: a case-insensitive '^revision' probe matches 92 lines instead of 46 (the 46 'Revision ID:' docstring lines plus the 46 assignments), so HEAD would read PRESENT, the control pair would not flip, and the check would be refused.

'A hand-written reader for five languages' overstates it. JSON is parsed, not lexed. SQL gets only '--' and '/* */' comment stripping, and YAML only block scalars. Python and TS/JS are the real lexers. ast-grep is also already named as the D5 alternative (l.265, l.693), so the critique asks for a different default, not for an option the design lacks.

'Exactly what fooled the text checks' overstates it. KS-C14 (l.786) records four ways the text checks were fooled: a guard that moved, comments quoting the bad code, a correct fix in the repo's own idiom (ex3 'clientId ?? crypto.randomUUID()'), and a neutraliser in another file (ex8). Ignoring comments and strings fixes one of the four. Symbol scoping, which the design already specifies, handles the moved guard. Nothing structural handles the other two. The KS-C6 repo refuter adds: 'The fallback variant defeats comment stripping anyway.'

'One pinned npm package' holds only for the CLI. In practice it is the CLI package plus a roughly 110 MB platform package, installed through a postinstall step. The in-process @ast-grep/napi has only Html, JavaScript, Tsx, Css and TypeScript built in, so Python, JSON and YAML would each need a 0.0.x @ast-grep/lang-* postinstall package. SQL is not built in on either route, and SQL inside a Python string is opaque to the Python parse.

The critique leaves out several costs. The latest release, 0.51.1, was published 2026-11-02, so the program's 14-day rule rules it out today (0.51.0 of 15 Oct qualifies). The binaries are unsigned, and Defender false-positived sg.exe in July 2026 (#2799 and #2841; the PR #2842 change shipped in 0.45.0). The box actually runs 360 Total Security (KS-C4), so whether the pinned binary gets flagged there is untested. The project is pre-1.0, effectively run by one maintainer, and 0.50.0 changed CLI behaviour. Telemetry-free rests on absence of evidence only.

'Never matches inside comments or strings' is true for pattern rules but not universal. A regex rule sees the matched node's whole text, comments included. At the default 'smart' strictness, a comment inside an argument list can make a fixed-arity pattern miss, which is a false absent. Tree-sitter recovers from syntax errors silently with ERROR nodes and zero-width MISSING nodes, so a parser can slip too unless an ERROR inside the probed span maps to inconclusive. The napi SgNode exposes no hasError or isMissing.
where_the_design_is_weak: Sequencing breaks the design's own rule. §0 l.39 says 'Code defects get their checks only after the pilot', and l.43 says it 'builds nothing before the pilot that the pilot does not need'. Yet KS-3, which is pre-pilot, builds the code-token lexer, symbol-span anchoring and the code mutants for ex1, ex3 and ex4. At pilot time those serve only the evidence lines and footprints of entries that cannot lead (KS-5 l.605 expects the lead-capable set to be ex7, ex2a, ex8 and the traps).

The lexer spec has gaps that this repo exercises: JSX text and JSX '{/* */}' comments, regex-versus-division after ')' or '=>', regex literals inside '${}', Python multi-line def signatures and string prefixes, and SQL embedded in Python strings. Of these, only the SQL-case and YAML-quoting mutants are tested at all.

The reading mode for duplicate_values is left undefined. It is the only lead-capable probe over Python (ex2a), and the doc never says whether it runs on raw text (fooled by comments and docstrings) or on lexed text (blind to the quoted revision ids). There is also no mode that keeps string values but drops comments, and no embedded-SQL mode for op.execute and sa.text arguments.

No rule says that a YAML or Python data value is lead-capable only when read by a real parser. A future YAML trap, for example in dependabot.yml, would be lead-capable under KS-F7 while being read by a hand lexer that handles only block scalars.

Lexer quality is never measured before the go decision. The fallback rate misses silent mis-spans and is read only at KS-9. Each lexer patch also changes runner_version, and every such change forces every control to be re-demonstrated (§5.1 trigger 5), so a hand lexer under repair churns the whole store.
result.strongest_counter_to_critique: Replacing the lexer with ast-grep does not move the safety bound the critique is worried about. Under KS-F7, a text probe over code can never produce a code-behaviour lead, whichever engine reads the text. That bound is set by test ids and db_probes, which are lexer-independent. A parser removes one of KS-C14's four fooling modes; symbol scoping, already in the design, handles a second, and nothing structural touches the other two (a correct fix in another idiom, a neutraliser in another file). Before the pilot no code-behaviour entry can lead at all (§0 l.39; KS-5 l.605), so the pilot needs neither a lexer nor ast-grep. Pushing ast-grep now would add an unsigned, pre-1.0, single-maintainer native binary with a history of antivirus false positives. On the cheaper napi route it would also need extra 0.0.x language packages, and SQL is missing on every route. All of that would arrive before the store has shown any value, which runs against the owner's rule of no installs without a decision.
result.strongest_counter_to_design: The design schedules a lexer for Python, TS/JS, YAML and SQL that nobody evaluated, and puts it in a pre-pilot phase that its own §0 says should not build machinery for code defects. The spec does not mention JSX, even though JobDetail.jsx, a precondition anchor, has 195 lines with '</'. It strips strings before probes, yet tests SQL that lives only inside Python strings (the ex4 guard is inside an f-string at 0046:56-61). It never defines how ex2a, its only lead-capable Python probe, reads text. Its one health metric cannot see a silently wrong span, and that metric is read only after the go/stop decision. A maintained parser was the register's own recommendation, and the critic who proposed the hand lexer said no lane had tested it.
result.recommended_action: One change, in three doc places. (1) §10 KS-3 and §3.4: take the code-token lexer, symbol-span anchoring and the ex1/ex3/ex4 code mutants out of KS-3 and move them to KS-6b. Before the pilot, declarative probes read only parsed data: JSON.parse for eas.json and app.json, lockfile JSON for dep_version. Add one narrow, fixture-pinned reader for ex2a: case-sensitive top-level revision/down_revision assignments outside the module docstring, with a golden fixture over all 46 migrations that asserts the 'Revision ID:' docstring lines do not count. Code-file footprints are whole-file blobs, which over-invalidate in the safe direction. (2) §11 D5: split ast-grep out and rule it at KS-6 start next to D9, so the owner gets no new touchpoint before the pilot. Change its default from 'hand lexer' to 'ast-grep CLI at an exact version at least 14 days old (today 0.51.0, not 0.51.1), sha256 recorded, version folded into runner_version, smoke-tested once on the box under 360 Total Security'. If the owner declines, build no code lexer: code-behaviour entries keep only executable checks and whole-file spans. (3) §3.4 rules for when structural probes land. KS-F7 stays verbatim. An ERROR node inside the probed span means inconclusive. SQL is read as the string argument of op.execute or sa.text, found by a Python rule and passed through a small case and comment normaliser; no SQL grammar is needed. A YAML or Python data value is lead-capable only through a real parse. The KS-9 metric becomes 'parse-error and unresolved-anchor rate'. §9 l.509 records that comment-awareness fixes one of KS-C14's four fooling modes, and that ex3 still takes P12a's test id.
result.cited_numbers_status: Point 0 cites no statistics. Its factual claims check out as follows. 'Five languages': the design lists five (l.265), but JSON is parsed, so four are lexed. 'One pinned npm package with a prebuilt Windows binary': supported for @ast-grep/cli 0.51.1 (exact-pinned win32-x64-msvc optional dependency, local-only postinstall), but it is really two packages, and napi needs extra language packages for Python, JSON and YAML. 0.51.1 is 1 day old, so it fails the 14-day rule; 0.51.0 passes. 'Maintained': supported (10 releases in about 23 weeks, MIT, 16k stars), but pre-1.0 and effectively one maintainer. 'Never matches inside comments or strings': supported for pattern rules, not for regex rules or tree-sitter error recovery. 'What fooled the text checks': one of four recorded fooling modes (KS-C14). Repo figures the lenses used and I re-checked at HEAD 3415b5e: AppContext.jsx:229 regex and the logPayment span at 312-328; States.jsx:19; Attendance.jsx:184; the 0046 f-string SQL at 56-61; 195 '</' lines in JobDetail.jsx; 37 op.execute calls in 21 migrations; 0 .sql files; '^revision' matches 46 lines case-sensitive and 92 case-insensitive. The other points' numbers (Facebook's ~10,000 and 99.9%, 19-23%, 10-18 points) are not part of this point. Per the research: 99.9% is supported ('almost'), ~10,000 is an order of magnitude only, and 10-18 points is a similar-versus-dissimilar gap for BM25 alone, not a keyword-versus-embedding gap.
